8014cb12ab.b: Graha-yuddha (amshu-vimarda) between śaniḥ and śukraḥ in rēvatī mīnaḥ, center-to-center separation 0°36′15.67″.
8014cb12ab.d:
This is an amshu-vimarda (a collision of rays -- the discs themselves do not touch): center-to-center separation 0°36′15.67″, 0°36′02.25″ apart, disc-to-disc. śaniḥ at rēvatī-4 mīnaḥ (latitude 2°15′32.13″ S, Rju (direct), magnitude +0.71, elongation 25°42′15.53″ W). śukraḥ at rēvatī-4 mīnaḥ (latitude 1°39′16.46″ S, Rju (direct), magnitude -3.87, elongation 25°39′41.05″ W). Classical texts weigh both the northern position and the greater apparent brightness/nearness in deciding the victor (jayI) of a yuddha; here śaniḥ is towards the north (traditionally said to prevail), while by brightness/nearness (the larger apparent diameter) śaniḥ is taken as jayI over śukraḥ. A graha-yuddha (also called amshu-vimarda, "collision of rays") occurs when two of the five tArA grahas -- budha, śukra, aṅgāraka, br̥haspati, śanaiśchara -- come within 1 aMsha (60 kalA) of each other in longitude, close enough that they may be difficult to tell apart in the sky. It is called yuddha proper only when their discs actually touch/overlap; otherwise, amshu-vimarda.

The Surya Siddhanta itself cautions that this matter is described only to indicate the auspicious/inauspicious effects for people -- in reality the grahas remain far apart from one another and continue along their own paths. This is not to be received with fear, but as an advance, compassionate intimation from those who calculated these movements accurately, meant to help people take protective measures in time.

Classical texts (e.g. Brihat Samhita ch. 17) weigh both which graha is to the north and which is more prominent (nearer/brighter, of larger apparent diameter) in declaring a victor (jayī) of the yuddha; the defeated (jita) graha's significations are said to suffer for a particular section of society -- this is never a universal ill effect. The traditional response is to increase one's spiritual efforts: japa, homa, dAna and parAyaNa (especially of the Navagraha stotra), with higher AvRtti for the two grahas actually involved, particularly if the day also coincides with some other puNya kAla (e.g. a sAyana saGkramaNa).

Per the Narada Samhita (as cited in Muhurta Chintamani), the nakshatra in which a graha-yuddha occurs should be avoided for auspicious functions (vivAha, upanayana etc.) for six months following the event. If this cannot be avoided, perform parihAra for candra-bala.

810a4dbfc1.b: Graha-yuddha (amshu-vimarda) between śaniḥ and śukraḥ in uttaraprōṣṭhapadā mīnaḥ, center-to-center separation 0°54′42.43″.
810a4dbfc1.d:
This is an amshu-vimarda (a collision of rays -- the discs themselves do not touch): center-to-center separation 0°54′42.43″, 0°54′29.66″ apart, disc-to-disc. śaniḥ at uttaraprōṣṭhapadā-2 mīnaḥ (latitude 2°07′32.73″ S, Rju (direct), magnitude +0.97, elongation 14°48′02.43″ E). śukraḥ at uttaraprōṣṭhapadā-2 mīnaḥ (latitude 1°12′50.30″ S, Rju (direct), magnitude -3.90, elongation 14°41′58.94″ E). Classical texts weigh both the northern position and the greater apparent brightness/nearness in deciding the victor (jayI) of a yuddha; here śaniḥ is towards the north (traditionally said to prevail), while by brightness/nearness (the larger apparent diameter) śaniḥ is taken as jayI over śukraḥ. A graha-yuddha (also called amshu-vimarda, "collision of rays") occurs when two of the five tArA grahas -- budha, śukra, aṅgāraka, br̥haspati, śanaiśchara -- come within 1 aMsha (60 kalA) of each other in longitude, close enough that they may be difficult to tell apart in the sky. It is called yuddha proper only when their discs actually touch/overlap; otherwise, amshu-vimarda.

The Surya Siddhanta itself cautions that this matter is described only to indicate the auspicious/inauspicious effects for people -- in reality the grahas remain far apart from one another and continue along their own paths. This is not to be received with fear, but as an advance, compassionate intimation from those who calculated these movements accurately, meant to help people take protective measures in time.

Classical texts (e.g. Brihat Samhita ch. 17) weigh both which graha is to the north and which is more prominent (nearer/brighter, of larger apparent diameter) in declaring a victor (jayī) of the yuddha; the defeated (jita) graha's significations are said to suffer for a particular section of society -- this is never a universal ill effect. The traditional response is to increase one's spiritual efforts: japa, homa, dAna and parAyaNa (especially of the Navagraha stotra), with higher AvRtti for the two grahas actually involved, particularly if the day also coincides with some other puNya kAla (e.g. a sAyana saGkramaNa).

Per the Narada Samhita (as cited in Muhurta Chintamani), the nakshatra in which a graha-yuddha occurs should be avoided for auspicious functions (vivAha, upanayana etc.) for six months following the event. If this cannot be avoided, perform parihAra for candra-bala.

Classical texts (e.g. Brihat Samhita ch. 17) weigh both which graha is to the north and which is more prominent (nearer/brighter, of larger apparent diameter) in declaring a victor (jayī) of the yuddha; the defeated (jita) graha's significations are said to suffer for a particular section of society -- this is never a universal ill effect. The traditional response is to increase one's spiritual efforts: japa, homa, dAna and parAyaNa (especially of the Navagraha stotra), with higher AvRtti for the two grahas actually involved, particularly if the day also coincides with some other puNya kAla (e.g. a sAyana saGkramaNa).

Per the Narada Samhita (as cited in Muhurta Chintamani), the nakshatra in which a graha-yuddha occurs should be avoided for auspicious functions (vivAha, upanayana etc.) for six months following the event. If this cannot be avoided, perform parihAra for candra-bala.
8121b7c7c4.s:
𑌭𑌾𑌵𑌾𑌭𑌾𑌵𑌾𑌯 𑌲𑍋𑌕𑌾𑌨𑌾𑌂 𑌕𑌲𑍍𑌪𑌨𑍇𑌯𑌂 𑌪𑍍𑌰𑌦𑌰𑍍𑌶𑌿𑌤𑌾।  
𑌸𑍍𑌵𑌮𑌾𑌰𑍍𑌗𑌗𑌾𑌃 𑌪𑍍𑌰𑌯𑌾𑌨𑍍𑌤𑍍𑌯𑍇𑌤𑍇 𑌦𑍂𑌰𑌮𑌨𑍍𑌯𑍋𑌨𑍍𑌯𑌮𑌾𑌶𑍍𑌰𑌿𑌤𑌾𑌃॥  
--𑌸𑍂𑌰𑍍𑌯𑌸𑌿𑌦𑍍𑌧𑌾𑌨𑍍𑌤𑍇  
  
𑌷𑌣𑍍𑌮𑌾𑌸𑌂 𑌗𑍍𑌰𑌹𑌭𑌿𑌨𑍍𑌨𑌭𑌂 𑌤𑍍𑌯𑌜 𑌶𑍁𑌭𑍇 𑌯𑍌𑌦𑍍𑌧𑌂 𑌤𑌥𑍋𑌤𑍍𑌪𑌾𑌤𑌭𑌮𑍍।  
--𑌮𑍁𑌹𑍂𑌰𑍍𑌤𑌚𑌿𑌨𑍍𑌤𑌾𑌮𑌣𑍌 (𑌨𑌾𑌰𑌦𑌸𑌂𑌹𑌿𑌤𑌾𑌨𑍁𑌸𑌾𑌰𑍇𑌣)

8128ce4237.b: Observed on Śukla-Trayōdaśī tithi of Vaiśākhaḥ (lunar) month (Sūryōdayaḥ/puurvaviddha).
8128ce4237.d: Last three days of vaiśākha-māsaḥ. anantaphaladam! Perform Shiva/Vishnu Puja, Bhagavata Parayanam, BhagavadGita Parayanam, Vishnu Sahasranama Parayanam, dāna of apūpa, pāyasa etc.
8128ce4237.s:
𑌯𑌃 𑌮𑌾𑌧𑌵𑍇 𑌵𑍈𑌶𑌾𑌖𑌮𑌾𑌸𑍇, 𑌤𑍍𑌰𑌯𑍋𑌦𑌶𑍀𑌚𑌤𑍁𑌰𑍍𑌦𑌶𑍀𑌪𑍂𑌰𑍍𑌣𑌿𑌮𑌾𑌸𑍁 𑌤𑌿𑌥𑌿𑌷𑍁 𑌸𑍍𑌨𑌾𑌨𑌾𑌦𑌿𑌕𑌂 𑌕𑌰𑍋𑌤𑌿  
𑌸 𑌨𑌿𑌶𑍍𑌚𑌯𑍇𑌨 𑌮𑍋𑌕𑍍𑌷𑌂 𑌪𑍍𑌰𑌾𑌪𑍍𑌨𑍁𑌯𑌾𑌤𑍍। 𑌯𑌥𑌾 𑌪𑍁𑌰𑌾 𑌧𑌨𑌶𑌰𑍍𑌮𑌾 𑌬𑍍𑌰𑌾𑌹𑍍𑌮𑌣𑌃 𑌤𑍍𑌰𑌯𑌃 𑌪𑍍𑌰𑍇𑌤𑌾𑌶𑍍𑌚  
𑌮𑍁𑌕𑍍𑌤𑌿𑌂 𑌪𑍍𑌰𑌾𑌪𑍁𑌰𑌿𑌤𑌿। 𑌅𑌤𑍍𑌰 𑌪𑍍𑌰𑌸𑌿𑌦𑍍𑌧𑌾 𑌕𑌥𑌾 𑌸𑌪𑍍𑌤𑌦𑌶𑌾𑌧𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌯𑌾𑌤𑍍𑌮𑌕𑌪𑌾𑌦𑍍𑌮𑍋𑌕𑍍𑌤𑌵𑍈𑌶𑌾𑌖𑌮𑌾𑌹𑌾𑌤𑍍𑌮𑍍𑌯𑍇।  
𑌪𑍁𑌰𑌾 𑌵𑌿𑌷𑍍𑌣𑍁𑌨𑌾 𑌤𑍍𑌰𑌯𑍋𑌦𑌶𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌂 𑌹𑌿𑌰𑌣𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌕𑍍𑌷𑌃, 𑌚𑌤𑍁𑌰𑍍𑌦𑌶𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌂 𑌮𑌧𑍁𑌶𑍍𑌚 𑌘𑌾𑌤𑌿𑌤𑌃,  
𑌪𑍌𑌰𑍍𑌣𑌮𑌾𑌸𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌂 𑌭𑍂𑌮𑍍𑌯𑍁𑌦𑍍𑌧𑌾𑌰𑌶𑍍𑌚 𑌕𑍃𑌤𑌃, 𑌤𑌤𑌃 𑌪𑍍𑌰𑌭𑍃𑌤𑌿 𑌤𑌾𑌸𑍍𑌤𑌿𑌥𑌯𑌃 𑌪𑍁𑌣𑍍𑌯𑌾 𑌜𑌾𑌤𑌾𑌃!  
𑌶𑍍𑌰𑍁𑌤𑌦𑍇𑌵 𑌉𑌵𑌾𑌚---  
𑌯𑌾𑌸𑍍𑌤𑌿𑌸𑍍𑌰𑌸𑍍𑌤𑌿𑌥𑌯𑌃 𑌪𑍁𑌣𑍍𑌯𑌾 𑌅𑌨𑍍𑌤𑌿𑌮𑌾𑌃 𑌶𑍁𑌕𑍍𑌲𑌪𑌕𑍍𑌷𑌕𑍇।  
𑌵𑍈𑌶𑌾𑌖𑌮𑌾𑌸𑌿 𑌰𑌾𑌜𑍇𑌨𑍍𑌦𑍍𑌰 𑌪𑍂𑌰𑍍𑌣𑌿𑌮𑌾𑌨𑍍𑌤𑌾𑌃 𑌶𑍁𑌭𑌾𑌵𑌹𑌾𑌃॥௧॥  
𑌅𑌨𑍍𑌤𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌃 𑌪𑍁𑌷𑍍𑌕𑌰𑌿𑌣𑍀𑌸𑌂𑌜𑍍𑌞𑌾𑌃 𑌸𑌰𑍍𑌵𑌪𑌾𑌪𑌕𑍍𑌷𑌯𑌾𑌵𑌹𑌾𑌃।  
𑌮𑌾𑌧𑌵𑍇 𑌮𑌾𑌸𑌿 𑌯𑌃 𑌪𑍂𑌰𑍍𑌣𑌂 𑌸𑍍𑌨𑌾𑌨𑌂 𑌕𑌰𑍍𑌤𑍁𑌂 𑌨 𑌚 𑌕𑍍𑌷𑌮𑌃॥௨॥  
𑌤𑌿𑌥𑌿𑌷𑍍𑌵𑍇𑌤𑌾𑌸𑍁 𑌸 𑌸𑍍𑌨𑌾𑌯𑌾𑌤𑍍𑌪𑍂𑌰𑍍𑌣𑌮𑍇𑌵 𑌫𑌲𑌂 𑌲𑌭𑍇𑌤𑍍।  
𑌸𑌰𑍍𑌵𑍇 𑌦𑍇𑌵𑌾𑌸𑍍𑌤𑍍𑌰𑌯𑍋𑌦𑌶𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌂 𑌸𑍍𑌥𑌿𑌤𑍍𑌵𑌾 𑌜𑌨𑍍𑌤𑍂𑌨𑍍𑌪𑍁𑌨𑌨𑍍𑌤𑌿 𑌹𑌿॥௩॥  
𑌪𑍂𑌰𑍍𑌣𑌾𑌯𑌾𑌃 𑌪𑌰𑍍𑌵𑌤𑍀𑌰𑍍𑌥𑍈𑌶𑍍𑌚 𑌵𑌿𑌷𑍍𑌣𑍁𑌨𑌾 𑌸𑌹 𑌸𑌂𑌸𑍍𑌥𑌿𑌤𑌾𑌃।  
𑌚𑌤𑍁𑌰𑍍𑌦𑌶𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌂 𑌸𑌯𑌜𑍍𑌞𑌾𑌶𑍍𑌚 𑌦𑍇𑌵𑌾 𑌏𑌤𑌾𑌨𑍍𑌪𑍁𑌨𑌨𑍍𑌤𑌿 𑌹𑌿॥௪॥  
𑌬𑍍𑌰𑌹𑍍𑌮𑌘𑍍𑌨𑌂 𑌵𑌾 𑌸𑍁𑌰𑌾𑌪𑌂 𑌵𑌾 𑌸𑌰𑍍𑌵𑌾𑌨𑍇𑌤𑌾𑌨𑍍𑌪𑍁𑌨𑌨𑍍𑌤𑌿 𑌹𑌿।  
𑌏𑌕𑌾𑌦𑌶𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌂 𑌪𑍁𑌰𑌾 𑌜𑌜𑍍𑌞𑍇 𑌵𑍈𑌶𑌾𑌖𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌮𑌮𑍃𑌤𑌂 𑌶𑍁𑌭𑌮𑍍॥௫॥  
𑌦𑍍𑌵𑌾𑌦𑌶𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌂 𑌪𑌾𑌲𑌿𑌤𑌂 𑌤𑌚𑍍𑌚 𑌵𑌿𑌷𑍍𑌣𑍁𑌨𑌾 𑌪𑍍𑌰𑌭𑌵𑌿𑌷𑍍𑌣𑍁𑌨𑌾।  
𑌤𑍍𑌰𑌯𑍋𑌦𑌶𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌂 𑌸𑍁𑌧𑌾𑌂 𑌦𑍇𑌵𑌾𑌨𑍍𑌪𑌾𑌯𑌯𑌾𑌮𑌾𑌸 𑌵𑍈 𑌹𑌰𑌿𑌃॥௬॥  
𑌜𑌘𑌾𑌨 𑌚 𑌚𑌤𑍁𑌰𑍍𑌦𑌶𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌂 𑌦𑍈𑌤𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌨𑍍𑌦𑍇𑌵𑌵𑌿𑌰𑍋𑌧𑌿𑌨𑌃।  
𑌪𑍂𑌰𑍍𑌣𑌾𑌯𑌾𑌂 𑌸𑌰𑍍𑌵𑌦𑍇𑌵𑌾𑌨𑌾𑌂 𑌸𑌾𑌮𑍍𑌰𑌾𑌜𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌪𑍍𑌤𑌿𑌰𑍍𑌬𑌭𑍂𑌵 𑌹॥௭॥  
𑌤𑌤𑍋 𑌦𑍇𑌵𑌾𑌃 𑌸𑍁𑌸𑌨𑍍𑌤𑍁𑌷𑍍𑌟𑌾 𑌏𑌤𑌾𑌸𑌾𑌂 𑌚 𑌵𑌰𑌂 𑌦𑌦𑍁𑌃।  
𑌤𑌿𑌸𑍃𑌣𑌾𑌂 𑌚 𑌤𑌿𑌥𑍀𑌨𑌾𑌂 𑌵𑍈 𑌪𑍍𑌰𑍀𑌤𑍍𑌯𑍋𑌤𑍍𑌫𑍁𑌲𑍍𑌲𑌵𑌿𑌲𑍋𑌚𑌨𑌾𑌃॥௮॥  
𑌏𑌤𑌾 𑌵𑍈𑌶𑌾𑌖𑌮𑌾𑌸𑌸𑍍𑌯 𑌤𑌿𑌸𑍍𑌰𑌶𑍍𑌚 𑌤𑌿𑌥𑌯𑌃 𑌶𑍁𑌭𑌾𑌃।  
𑌪𑍁𑌤𑍍𑌰𑌪𑍌𑌤𑍍𑌰𑌾𑌦𑌿𑌫𑌲𑌦𑌾 𑌨𑌰𑌾𑌣𑌾𑌂 𑌪𑌾𑌪𑌹𑌾𑌨𑌿𑌦𑌾𑌃॥௯॥  
𑌯𑍋𑌽𑌸𑍍𑌮𑌿𑌨𑍍𑌮𑌾𑌸𑍇 𑌚 𑌸𑌮𑍍𑌪𑍂𑌰𑍍𑌣𑍇 𑌨 𑌸𑍍𑌨𑌾𑌤𑍋 𑌮𑌨𑍁𑌜𑌾𑌧𑌮𑌃।  
𑌤𑌿𑌥𑌿𑌤𑍍𑌰𑌯𑍇 𑌤𑍁 𑌸 𑌸𑍍𑌨𑌾𑌤𑍍𑌵𑌾 𑌪𑍂𑌰𑍍𑌣𑌮𑍇𑌵 𑌫𑌲𑌂 𑌲𑌭𑍇𑌤𑍍॥௧௦॥  
𑌤𑌿𑌥𑌿𑌤𑍍𑌰𑌯𑍇𑌽𑌪𑍍𑌯𑌕𑍁𑌰𑍍𑌵𑌾𑌣𑌃 𑌸𑍍𑌨𑌾𑌨𑌦𑌾𑌨𑌾𑌦𑌿𑌕𑌂 𑌨𑌰𑌃।  
𑌚𑌾𑌣𑍍𑌡𑌾𑌲𑍀𑌂 𑌯𑍋𑌨𑌿𑌮𑌾𑌸𑌾𑌦𑍍𑌯 𑌪𑌶𑍍𑌚𑌾𑌦𑍍𑌰𑍌𑌰𑌵𑌮𑌶𑍍𑌨𑍁𑌤𑍇॥௧௧॥  
𑌉𑌷𑍍𑌣𑍋𑌦𑌕𑍇𑌨 𑌯𑌃 𑌸𑍍𑌨𑌾𑌤𑌿 𑌮𑌾𑌧𑌵𑍇 𑌚 𑌤𑌿𑌥𑌿𑌤𑍍𑌰𑌯𑍇।  
𑌰𑍌𑌰𑌵𑌂 𑌨𑌰𑌕𑌂 𑌯𑌾𑌤𑌿 𑌯𑌾𑌵𑌦𑌿𑌨𑍍𑌦𑍍𑌰𑌾𑌶𑍍𑌚𑌤𑍁𑌰𑍍𑌦𑌶॥௧௨॥  
𑌪𑌿𑌤𑍄𑌨𑍍𑌦𑍇𑌵𑌾𑌨𑍍𑌸𑌮𑍁𑌦𑍍𑌦𑌿𑌶𑍍𑌯 𑌦𑌧𑍍𑌯𑌨𑍍𑌨𑌂 𑌨 𑌦𑌦𑌾𑌤𑌿 𑌯𑌃।  
𑌪𑍈𑌶𑌾𑌚𑍀𑌂 𑌯𑍋𑌨𑌿𑌮𑌾𑌸𑌾𑌦𑍍𑌯 𑌤𑌿𑌷𑍍𑌠𑌤𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌭𑍂𑌤𑌸𑌮𑍍𑌪𑍍𑌲𑌵𑌮𑍍॥௧௩॥  
𑌪𑍍𑌰𑌵𑍃𑌤𑍍𑌤𑌾𑌨𑌾𑌂 𑌚 𑌕𑌾𑌮𑌾𑌨𑌾𑌂 𑌮𑌾𑌧𑌵𑍇 𑌨𑌿𑌯𑌮𑍇 𑌕𑍃𑌤𑍇।  
𑌅𑌵𑌶𑍍𑌯𑌂 𑌵𑌿𑌷𑍍𑌣𑍁𑌸𑌾𑌯𑍁𑌜𑍍𑌯𑌂 𑌯𑍁𑌜𑍍𑌯𑌤𑍇 𑌨𑌾𑌤𑍍𑌰 𑌸𑌂𑌶𑌯𑌃॥௧௪॥  
𑌆𑌮𑌾𑌸𑌂 𑌨𑌿𑌯𑌮𑌾𑌸𑌕𑍍𑌤𑌃 𑌕𑍁𑌰𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌦𑍍𑌯𑌦𑌿 𑌦𑌿𑌨𑌤𑍍𑌰𑌯𑍇।  
𑌤𑍇𑌨 𑌪𑍂𑌰𑍍𑌣𑌫𑌲𑌂 𑌪𑍍𑌰𑌾𑌪𑍍𑌯 𑌮𑍋𑌦𑌤𑍇 𑌵𑌿𑌷𑍍𑌣𑍁𑌮𑌨𑍍𑌦𑌿𑌰𑍇॥௧௫॥  
𑌯𑍋 𑌵𑍈 𑌦𑍇𑌵𑌾𑌨𑍍𑌪𑌿𑌤𑍄𑌨𑍍𑌵𑌿𑌷𑍍𑌣𑍁𑌂 𑌗𑍁𑌰𑍁𑌮𑍁𑌦𑍍𑌦𑌿𑌶𑍍𑌯 𑌮𑌾𑌨𑌵𑌃।  
𑌨 𑌸𑍍𑌨𑌾𑌨𑌾𑌦𑌿 𑌕𑌰𑍋𑌤𑍍𑌯𑌦𑍍𑌧𑌾𑌽𑌮𑍁𑌷𑍍𑌯 𑌶𑌾𑌪𑌪𑍍𑌰𑌦𑌾 𑌵𑌯𑌮𑍍॥௧௬॥  
𑌨𑌿𑌃𑌸𑌨𑍍𑌤𑌾𑌨𑍋 𑌨𑌿𑌰𑌾𑌯𑍁𑌶𑍍𑌚 𑌨𑌿𑌃𑌶𑍍𑌰𑍇𑌯𑌸𑍍𑌕𑍋 𑌭𑌵𑍇𑌦𑌿𑌤𑌿।  
𑌇𑌤𑌿 𑌦𑍇𑌵𑌾 𑌵𑌰𑌂 𑌦𑌤𑍍𑌤𑍍𑌵𑌾 𑌸𑍍𑌵𑌧𑌾𑌮𑌾𑌨𑌿 𑌯𑌯𑍁𑌃 𑌪𑍁𑌰𑌾॥௧௭॥  
𑌤𑌸𑍍𑌮𑌾𑌤𑍍𑌤𑌿𑌥𑌿𑌤𑍍𑌰𑌯𑌂 𑌪𑍁𑌣𑍍𑌯𑌂 𑌸𑌰𑍍𑌵𑌾𑌘𑍌𑌘𑌵𑌿𑌨𑌾𑌶𑌨𑌮𑍍।  
𑌅𑌨𑍍𑌤𑍍𑌯𑌂 𑌪𑍁𑌷𑍍𑌕𑌰𑌿𑌣𑍀𑌸𑌂𑌜𑍍𑌞𑌂 𑌪𑍁𑌤𑍍𑌰𑌪𑍌𑌤𑍍𑌰𑌵𑌿𑌵𑌰𑍍𑌧𑌨𑌮𑍍॥௧௮॥  
𑌯𑌾 𑌨𑌾𑌰𑍀 𑌸𑍁𑌭𑌗𑌾𑌽𑌪𑍂𑌪𑌪𑌾𑌯𑌸𑌂 𑌪𑍂𑌰𑍍𑌣𑌿𑌮𑌾𑌦𑌿𑌨𑍇।  
𑌬𑍍𑌰𑌾𑌹𑍍𑌮𑌣𑌾𑌯 𑌸𑌕𑍃𑌦𑍍𑌦𑌦𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌤𑍍𑌕𑍀𑌰𑍍𑌤𑌿𑌮𑌨𑍍𑌤𑌂 𑌸𑍁𑌤𑌂 𑌲𑌭𑍇𑌤𑍍॥௧௯॥  
𑌗𑍀𑌤𑌾𑌪𑌾𑌠𑌂 𑌤𑍁 𑌯𑌃 𑌕𑍁𑌰𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌦𑌨𑍍𑌤𑌿𑌮𑍇 𑌚 𑌦𑌿𑌨𑌤𑍍𑌰𑌯𑍇।  
𑌦𑌿𑌨𑍇𑌦𑌿𑌨𑍇𑌽𑌶𑍍𑌵𑌮𑍇𑌧𑌾𑌨𑌾𑌂 𑌫𑌲𑌮𑍇𑌤𑌿 𑌨 𑌸𑌂𑌶𑌯𑌃॥௨௦॥  
𑌸𑌹𑌸𑍍𑌰𑌨𑌾𑌮𑌪𑌠𑌨𑌂 𑌯𑌃 𑌕𑍁𑌰𑍍𑌯𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌚𑍍𑌚 𑌦𑌿𑌨𑌤𑍍𑌰𑌯𑍇।  
𑌤𑌸𑍍𑌯 𑌪𑍁𑌣𑍍𑌯𑌫𑌲𑌂 𑌵𑌕𑍍𑌤𑍁𑌂 𑌕𑌃 𑌶𑌕𑍍𑌤𑍋 𑌦𑌿𑌵𑌿 𑌵𑌾 𑌭𑍁𑌵𑌿॥௨௧॥  
𑌸𑌹𑌸𑍍𑌰𑌨𑌾𑌮𑌭𑌿𑌰𑍍𑌦𑍇𑌵𑌂 𑌪𑍂𑌰𑍍𑌣𑌾𑌯𑌾𑌂 𑌮𑌧𑍁𑌸𑍂𑌦𑌨𑌮𑍍।  
𑌪𑌯𑌸𑌾 𑌸𑍍𑌨𑌾𑌪𑍍𑌯 𑌵𑍈 𑌯𑌾𑌤𑌿 𑌵𑌿𑌷𑍍𑌣𑍁𑌲𑍋𑌕𑌮𑌕𑌲𑍍𑌮𑌷𑌮𑍍॥௨௨॥  
𑌸𑌮𑌸𑍍𑌤𑌵𑌿𑌭𑌵𑍈𑌰𑍍𑌯𑌸𑍍𑌤𑍁 𑌪𑍂𑌜𑌯𑍇𑌨𑍍𑌮𑌧𑍁𑌸𑍂𑌦𑌨𑌮𑍍।  
𑌨 𑌤𑌸𑍍𑌯 𑌲𑍋𑌕𑌾𑌃 𑌕𑍍𑌷𑍀𑌯𑌨𑍍𑌤𑍇 𑌯𑍁𑌗 𑌕𑌲𑍍𑌪𑌾𑌦𑌿 𑌵𑍍𑌯𑌤𑍍𑌯𑌯𑍇॥௨௩॥  
𑌅𑌸𑍍𑌨𑌾𑌤𑍍𑌵𑌾 𑌚𑌾𑌪𑍍𑌯𑌦𑌤𑍍𑌤𑍍𑌵𑌾 𑌚 𑌵𑍈𑌶𑌾𑌖𑌶𑍍𑌚 𑌮𑌤𑍋 𑌯𑌦𑌿।  
𑌸 𑌬𑍍𑌰𑌹𑍍𑌮𑌹𑌾 𑌗𑍁𑌰𑍁𑌘𑍍𑌨𑌶𑍍𑌚 𑌪𑌿𑌤𑍄𑌣𑌾𑌂 𑌘𑌾𑌤𑌕𑌸𑍍𑌤𑌥𑌾॥௨௪॥  
𑌶𑍍𑌲𑍋𑌕𑌾𑌰𑍍𑌧𑌂 𑌶𑍍𑌲𑍋𑌕𑌪𑌾𑌦𑌂 𑌵𑌾 𑌨𑌿𑌤𑍍𑌯𑌂 𑌭𑌾𑌗𑌵𑌤𑍋𑌦𑍍𑌭𑌵𑌮𑍍।  
𑌵𑍈𑌶𑌾𑌖𑍇 𑌚 𑌪𑌠𑌨𑍍𑌮𑌰𑍍𑌤𑍍𑌯𑍋 𑌬𑍍𑌰𑌹𑍍𑌮𑌤𑍍𑌵𑌂 𑌚𑍋𑌪𑌪𑌦𑍍𑌯𑌤𑍇॥௨௫॥  
𑌯𑍋 𑌵𑍈 𑌭𑌾𑌗𑌵𑌤𑌂 𑌶𑌾𑌸𑍍𑌤𑍍𑌰𑌂 𑌶𑍃𑌣𑍋𑌤𑍍𑌯𑍇𑌤𑌦𑍍𑌦𑌿𑌨𑌤𑍍𑌰𑌯𑍇।  
𑌨 𑌪𑌾𑌪𑍈𑌰𑍍𑌲𑌿𑌪𑍍𑌯𑌤𑍇 𑌕𑍍𑌵𑌾𑌪𑌿 𑌪𑌦𑍍𑌮𑌪𑌤𑍍𑌰𑌮𑌿𑌵𑌾𑌮𑍍𑌭𑌸𑌾॥௨௬॥  
𑌦𑍇𑌵𑌤𑍍𑌵𑌂 𑌮𑌨𑍁𑌜𑍈𑌃 𑌪𑍍𑌰𑌾𑌪𑍍𑌤𑌂 𑌕𑍈𑌶𑍍𑌚𑌿𑌤𑍍𑌸𑌿𑌦𑍍𑌧𑌤𑍍𑌵𑌮𑍇𑌵 𑌚।  
𑌕𑍈𑌶𑍍𑌚𑌿𑌤𑍍𑌪𑍍𑌰𑌾𑌪𑍍𑌤𑍋 𑌬𑍍𑌰𑌹𑍍𑌮𑌭𑌾𑌵𑍋 𑌦𑌿𑌨𑌤𑍍𑌰𑌯𑌨𑌿𑌷𑍇𑌵𑌣𑌾𑌤𑍍॥௨௭॥  
𑌬𑍍𑌰𑌹𑍍𑌮𑌜𑍍𑌞𑌾𑌨𑍇𑌨 𑌵𑍈 𑌮𑍁𑌕𑍍𑌤𑌿𑌃 𑌪𑍍𑌰𑌯𑌾𑌗𑌮𑌰𑌣𑍇𑌨 𑌵𑌾।  
𑌅𑌥𑌵𑌾 𑌮𑌾𑌸𑌿 𑌵𑍈𑌶𑌾𑌖𑍇 𑌨𑌿𑌯𑌮𑍇𑌨 𑌜𑌲𑌾𑌪𑍍𑌲𑍁𑌤𑍇𑌃॥௨௮॥  
𑌨𑍀𑌲𑌵𑍃𑌷𑌂 𑌸𑌮𑍁𑌤𑍍𑌸𑍃𑌜𑍍𑌯 𑌵𑍈𑌶𑌾𑌖𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌂 𑌚 𑌜𑌲𑌾𑌪𑍍𑌲𑍁𑌤𑍇𑌃।  
𑌸𑌮𑌸𑍍𑌤𑌬𑌨𑍍𑌧𑌨𑌿𑌰𑍍𑌮𑍁𑌕𑍍𑌤𑌃 𑌪𑍁𑌮𑌾𑌨𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌤𑌿 𑌪𑌰𑌂 𑌪𑌦𑌮𑍍॥௨௯॥  
𑌗𑌾𑌂 𑌸𑌵𑌤𑍍𑌸𑌾𑌂 𑌦𑍍𑌵𑌿𑌜𑍇𑌨𑍍𑌦𑍍𑌰𑌾𑌯 𑌸𑍀𑌦𑌤𑍇 𑌚 𑌕𑍁𑌟𑍁𑌮𑍍𑌬𑌿𑌨𑍇।  
𑌇𑌹𑌾𑌪𑌮𑍃𑌤𑍍𑌯𑍁𑌨𑌿𑌰𑍍𑌮𑍁𑌕𑍍𑌤𑌃 𑌪𑌰𑌤𑍍𑌰 𑌚 𑌪𑌰𑌂 𑌵𑍍𑌰𑌜𑍇𑌤𑍍॥௩௦॥  
𑌸𑍍𑌨𑌾𑌨𑌦𑌾𑌨𑌵𑌿𑌹𑍀𑌨𑌸𑍍𑌤𑍁 𑌵𑍈𑌶𑌾𑌖𑍀 𑌚𑍈𑌵 𑌯𑍋 𑌨𑌯𑍇𑌤𑍍।  
𑌶𑍍𑌵𑌾𑌨𑌯𑍋𑌨𑌿𑌶𑌤𑌂 𑌪𑍍𑌰𑌾𑌪𑍍𑌯 𑌵𑌿𑌷𑍍𑌠𑌾𑌯𑌾𑌂 𑌜𑌾𑌯𑌤𑍇 𑌕𑍃𑌮𑌿𑌃॥௩௧॥  
𑌤𑌿𑌸𑍍𑌰𑌃 𑌕𑍋𑌟𑍍𑌯𑍋𑌽𑌰𑍍𑌧𑌕𑍋𑌟𑌿𑌶𑍍𑌚 𑌤𑍀𑌰𑍍𑌥𑌾𑌨𑌿 𑌭𑍁𑌵𑌨𑌤𑍍𑌰𑌯𑍇।  
𑌸𑌮𑍍𑌭𑍂𑌯 𑌮𑌨𑍍𑌤𑍍𑌰𑌯𑌾𑌞𑍍𑌚𑌕𑍍𑌰𑍁𑌃 𑌪𑌾𑌪𑌸𑌙𑍍𑌘𑌾𑌤𑌶𑌙𑍍𑌕𑌿𑌤𑌾𑌃॥௩௨॥  
𑌜𑌨𑌾 𑌅𑌸𑍍𑌮𑌾𑌸𑍁 𑌪𑌾𑌪𑌿𑌷𑍍𑌠𑌾 𑌵𑌿𑌸𑍃𑌜𑌨𑍍𑌤𑌿 𑌸𑍍𑌵𑌕𑌂 𑌮𑌲𑌮𑍍।  
𑌤𑌦𑌸𑍍𑌮𑌾𑌕𑌂 𑌕𑌥𑌂 𑌗𑌚𑍍𑌛𑍇𑌦𑌿𑌤𑌿 𑌚𑌿𑌨𑍍𑌤𑌾𑌸𑌮𑌨𑍍𑌵𑌿𑌤𑌾𑌃॥௩௩॥  
𑌤𑍀𑌰𑍍𑌥𑌪𑌾𑌦𑌂 𑌹𑌰𑌿𑌂 𑌜𑌗𑍍𑌮𑍁𑌃 𑌶𑌰𑌣𑍍𑌯𑌂 𑌶𑌰𑌣𑌂 𑌵𑌿𑌭𑍁𑌮𑍍।  
𑌸𑍍𑌤𑍁𑌤𑍍𑌵𑌾 𑌚 𑌬𑌹𑍁𑌭𑌿𑌃 𑌸𑍍𑌤𑍋𑌤𑍍𑌰𑍈𑌃 𑌪𑍍𑌰𑌾𑌰𑍍𑌥𑌯𑌾𑌮𑌾𑌸𑍁𑌰𑌞𑍍𑌜𑌸𑌾॥௩௪॥  
𑌦𑍇𑌵𑌦𑍇𑌵 𑌜𑌗𑌨𑍍𑌨𑌾𑌥 𑌸𑌰𑍍𑌵𑌾𑌘𑍌𑌘𑌵𑌿𑌨𑌾𑌶𑌨।  
𑌜𑌨𑌾 𑌅𑌸𑍍𑌮𑌾𑌸𑍁 𑌪𑌾𑌪𑌿𑌷𑍍𑌠𑌾𑌃 𑌸𑍍𑌨𑌾𑌤𑍍𑌵𑌾 𑌪𑌾𑌪𑌾𑌨𑌿 𑌸𑌰𑍍𑌵𑌶𑌃॥௩௫॥  
𑌵𑌿𑌸𑍃𑌜𑍍𑌯 𑌤𑍍𑌵𑌤𑍍𑌪𑌦𑌂 𑌯𑌾𑌨𑍍𑌤𑌿 𑌤𑍍𑌵𑌦𑌾𑌜𑍍𑌞𑌾𑌧𑌾𑌰𑌿𑌣𑍋 𑌭𑍁𑌵𑌿।  
𑌅𑌸𑍍𑌮𑌾𑌕𑌂 𑌚𑍈𑌵 𑌤𑌤𑍍𑌪𑌾𑌪𑌂 𑌕𑌥𑌂 𑌗𑌚𑍍𑌛𑍇𑌜𑍍𑌜𑌨𑌾𑌰𑍍𑌦𑌨॥௩௬॥  
𑌤𑌦𑍁𑌪𑌾𑌯𑌂 𑌵𑌦𑌾𑌸𑍍𑌮𑌾𑌕𑌂 𑌤𑍍𑌵𑌤𑍍𑌪𑌾𑌦𑌶𑌰𑌣𑍈𑌷𑌿𑌣𑌾𑌮𑍍।  
𑌇𑌤𑌿 𑌤𑍀𑌰𑍍𑌥𑍈𑌃 𑌪𑍍𑌰𑌾𑌰𑍍𑌥𑌿𑌤𑌸𑍍𑌤𑍁 𑌭𑌗𑌵𑌾𑌨𑍍𑌭𑍂𑌤𑌭𑌾𑌵𑌨𑌃॥௩௭॥  
𑌪𑍍𑌰𑌹𑌸𑌨𑍍𑌪𑍍𑌰𑌾𑌹 𑌤𑍀𑌰𑍍𑌥𑌾𑌨𑌿 𑌮𑍇𑌘𑌗𑌮𑍍𑌭𑍀𑌰𑌯𑌾 𑌗𑌿𑌰𑌾।  
𑌶𑍍𑌰𑍀𑌭𑌗𑌵𑌾𑌨𑍁𑌵𑌾𑌚---  
𑌸𑌿𑌤𑍇 𑌪𑌕𑍍𑌷𑍇 𑌮𑍇𑌷𑌸𑍂𑌰𑍍𑌯𑍇 𑌵𑍈𑌶𑌾𑌖𑌾𑌨𑍍𑌤𑍇𑌦𑌿𑌨𑌤𑍍𑌰𑌯𑍇॥௩௮॥  
𑌸𑌰𑍍𑌵𑌤𑍀𑌰𑍍𑌥𑌮𑌯𑍇 𑌪𑍁𑌣𑍍𑌯𑍇 𑌮𑌮𑌾𑌪𑌿 𑌪𑍍𑌰𑌾𑌣𑌵𑌲𑍍𑌲𑌭𑍇।  
𑌯𑍂𑌯𑌂 𑌭𑌗𑍋𑌦𑌯𑌾𑌤𑍍𑌪𑍂𑌰𑍍𑌵𑌂 𑌬𑌹𑌿𑌃𑌸𑌂𑌸𑍍𑌥𑌜𑌲𑌾𑌪𑍍𑌲𑍁𑌤𑌾𑌃॥௩௯॥  
𑌵𑌿𑌮𑍁𑌕𑍍𑌤𑌾𑌘𑌾𑌃 𑌪𑍁𑌣𑍍𑌯𑌰𑍂𑌪𑌾 𑌭𑌵𑌨𑍍𑌤𑍍𑌵𑌾𑌶𑍁 𑌸𑍁𑌨𑌿𑌰𑍍𑌮𑌲𑌾𑌃।  
𑌭𑌵𑌦𑍍𑌭𑌿𑌶𑍍𑌚 𑌵𑌿𑌮𑍁𑌕𑍍𑌤𑌾𑌘𑍈𑌰𑍍𑌯𑍇 𑌨 𑌸𑍍𑌨𑌾𑌤𑌾 𑌦𑌿𑌨𑌤𑍍𑌰𑌯𑍇॥௪௦॥  
𑌤𑍇𑌷𑍁 𑌤𑌿𑌷𑍍𑌠𑌨𑍍𑌤𑍁 𑌤𑌤𑍍𑌪𑌾𑌪𑌂 𑌜𑌨𑍈𑌰𑍍𑌯𑍁𑌷𑍍𑌮𑌦𑍍𑌵𑌿𑌰𑍇𑌚𑌿𑌤𑌮𑍍।  
𑌇𑌤𑌿 𑌤𑍀𑌰𑍍𑌥𑌪𑌦𑍋 𑌵𑌿𑌷𑍍𑌣𑍁𑌸𑍍𑌤𑍀𑌰𑍍𑌥𑌾𑌨𑌾𑌂 𑌚 𑌵𑌰𑌂 𑌦𑌦𑍌॥௪௧॥  
𑌅𑌨𑍁𑌜𑍍𑌞𑌾𑌪𑍍𑌯 𑌚 𑌤𑌾𑌨𑍍𑌯𑍋𑌗𑌾𑌤𑍍𑌤𑌤𑍍𑌰𑍈𑌵𑌾𑌨𑍍𑌤𑌰𑌧𑍀𑌯𑌤।  
𑌸𑍍𑌵𑌧𑌾𑌮𑌾𑌨𑌿 𑌪𑍁𑌨𑌃 𑌪𑍍𑌰𑌾𑌪𑍍𑌯 𑌤𑌾𑌨𑌿 𑌤𑍀𑌰𑍍𑌥𑌾𑌨𑌿 𑌨𑌿𑌤𑍍𑌯𑌶𑌃॥௪௨॥

81a86d4a56.b: Graha-yuddha (amshu-vimarda) between śaniḥ and śukraḥ in uttaraprōṣṭhapadā mīnaḥ, center-to-center separation 0°54′41.97″.
81a86d4a56.d:
This is an amshu-vimarda (a collision of rays -- the discs themselves do not touch): center-to-center separation 0°54′41.97″, 0°54′29.20″ apart, disc-to-disc. śaniḥ at uttaraprōṣṭhapadā-2 mīnaḥ (latitude 2°07′32.83″ S, Rju (direct), magnitude +0.97, elongation 14°48′02.50″ E). śukraḥ at uttaraprōṣṭhapadā-2 mīnaḥ (latitude 1°12′50.86″ S, Rju (direct), magnitude -3.90, elongation 14°41′59.10″ E). Classical texts weigh both the northern position and the greater apparent brightness/nearness in deciding the victor (jayI) of a yuddha; here śaniḥ is towards the north (traditionally said to prevail), while by brightness/nearness (the larger apparent diameter) śaniḥ is taken as jayI over śukraḥ. A graha-yuddha (also called amshu-vimarda, "collision of rays") occurs when two of the five tArA grahas -- budha, śukra, aṅgāraka, br̥haspati, śanaiśchara -- come within 1 aMsha (60 kalA) of each other in longitude, close enough that they may be difficult to tell apart in the sky. It is called yuddha proper only when their discs actually touch/overlap; otherwise, amshu-vimarda.

The Surya Siddhanta itself cautions that this matter is described only to indicate the auspicious/inauspicious effects for people -- in reality the grahas remain far apart from one another and continue along their own paths. This is not to be received with fear, but as an advance, compassionate intimation from those who calculated these movements accurately, meant to help people take protective measures in time.

Classical texts (e.g. Brihat Samhita ch. 17) weigh both which graha is to the north and which is more prominent (nearer/brighter, of larger apparent diameter) in declaring a victor (jayī) of the yuddha; the defeated (jita) graha's significations are said to suffer for a particular section of society -- this is never a universal ill effect. The traditional response is to increase one's spiritual efforts: japa, homa, dAna and parAyaNa (especially of the Navagraha stotra), with higher AvRtti for the two grahas actually involved, particularly if the day also coincides with some other puNya kAla (e.g. a sAyana saGkramaNa).

Per the Narada Samhita (as cited in Muhurta Chintamani), the nakshatra in which a graha-yuddha occurs should be avoided for auspicious functions (vivAha, upanayana etc.) for six months following the event. If this cannot be avoided, perform parihAra for candra-bala.

829a2d59f3.b: Graha-yuddha (amshu-vimarda) between guruḥ and budhaḥ in maghā siṁhaḥ, center-to-center separation 0°37′24.41″.
829a2d59f3.d:
This is an amshu-vimarda (a collision of rays -- the discs themselves do not touch): center-to-center separation 0°37′24.41″, 0°37′06.85″ apart, disc-to-disc. guruḥ at maghā-4 siṁhaḥ (latitude 0°54′43.40″ N, Rju (direct), magnitude -1.70, elongation 8°32′36.90″ E). budhaḥ at maghā-4 siṁhaḥ (latitude 1°32′07.81″ N, Rju (direct), magnitude -1.11, elongation 8°37′54.37″ E). Classical texts weigh both the northern position and the greater apparent brightness/nearness in deciding the victor (jayI) of a yuddha; here budhaḥ is towards the north (traditionally said to prevail), while by brightness/nearness (the larger apparent diameter) guruḥ is taken as jayI over budhaḥ. A graha-yuddha (also called amshu-vimarda, "collision of rays") occurs when two of the five tArA grahas -- budha, śukra, aṅgāraka, br̥haspati, śanaiśchara -- come within 1 aMsha (60 kalA) of each other in longitude, close enough that they may be difficult to tell apart in the sky. It is called yuddha proper only when their discs actually touch/overlap; otherwise, amshu-vimarda.

The Surya Siddhanta itself cautions that this matter is described only to indicate the auspicious/inauspicious effects for people -- in reality the grahas remain far apart from one another and continue along their own paths. This is not to be received with fear, but as an advance, compassionate intimation from those who calculated these movements accurately, meant to help people take protective measures in time.

Classical texts (e.g. Brihat Samhita ch. 17) weigh both which graha is to the north and which is more prominent (nearer/brighter, of larger apparent diameter) in declaring a victor (jayī) of the yuddha; the defeated (jita) graha's significations are said to suffer for a particular section of society -- this is never a universal ill effect. The traditional response is to increase one's spiritual efforts: japa, homa, dAna and parAyaNa (especially of the Navagraha stotra), with higher AvRtti for the two grahas actually involved, particularly if the day also coincides with some other puNya kAla (e.g. a sAyana saGkramaNa).

Per the Narada Samhita (as cited in Muhurta Chintamani), the nakshatra in which a graha-yuddha occurs should be avoided for auspicious functions (vivAha, upanayana etc.) for six months following the event. If this cannot be avoided, perform parihAra for candra-bala.

82b35ee28b.b: Observed on Paurṇamāsī tithi of every (lunar) month (Sāṅgavaḥ/paraviddha).
82b35ee28b.d: Anadhyayana on account of pūrṇimā. Several tithis in a month are nitya-anadhyayana days, including prathamā, aṣṭamī, chaturdaśī, amāvāsyā and pūrṇimā. Manu has said that performing adhyayana on these days destroys the Guru (Amavasya), Shishya (Chaturdashi) and the vīrya of the brahma (vēda) itself (Ashtami/Purnima). Similarly, Jabali Rishi has said that Adhyayana on prathama hurts the buddhi while adhyayana on chaturdaśī hurts the brahma (vēda) itself!
82b35ee28b.s:
𑌹𑌾𑌰𑍀𑌤𑌃—  
𑌪𑍍𑌰𑌤𑌿𑌪𑌤𑍍𑌸𑍁 𑌚𑌤𑍁𑌰𑍍𑌦𑌶𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌮𑌷𑍍𑌟𑌮𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌂 𑌪𑌰𑍍𑌵𑌣𑍋𑌰𑍍𑌦𑍍𑌵𑌯𑍋𑌃।

𑌮𑌨𑍁𑌃—  
𑌅𑌮𑌾𑌵𑌾𑌸𑍍𑌯𑌾 𑌗𑍁𑌰𑍁𑌂 𑌹𑌨𑍍𑌤𑌿 𑌶𑌿𑌷𑍍𑌯𑌂 𑌹𑌨𑍍𑌤𑌿 𑌚𑌤𑍁𑌰𑍍𑌦𑌶𑍀।  
𑌬𑍍𑌰𑌹𑍍𑌮𑌾𑌷𑍍𑌟𑌕𑌾𑌪𑍌𑌰𑍍𑌣𑌮𑌾𑌸𑍍𑌯𑌸𑍍𑌤𑌸𑍍𑌮𑌾𑌤𑍍𑌤𑌾𑌃 𑌪𑌰𑌿𑌵𑌰𑍍𑌜𑌯𑍇𑌦𑌿𑌤𑌿॥  
𑌯𑌾𑌜𑍍𑌞𑌵𑌲𑍍𑌕𑍍𑌯𑌃—  
𑌪𑌞𑍍𑌚𑌦𑌶𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌂 𑌚𑌤𑍁𑌰𑍍𑌦𑌶𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌂 𑌅𑌷𑍍𑌟𑌮𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌂 𑌰𑌾𑌹𑍁𑌸𑍂𑌤𑌕𑍇।

83bc8a5a5b.d:
A massacre and gang rape of the emigrating Hindus of the then Dinajpur district near Baraihat on 17 April 1971 by the Pakistani army with collaboration from the local Razakars.

Events
In April 1971, a member of the Razakar forces, Kenan Uddin Sarkar of Ramchandrapur village under Parbatipur sub-division of Dinajpur district, assured 50 Hindu families of neighbouring Badarganj, Kholahati, Birampur, Aftabganj and Sherpur of a safe passage to India. He kept the Hindus confined at a place called Baraihat in present-day Phulbari Upazila. The Razakars and the Al-Badr militia looted the money and jewelry from Hindus during their confinement. After that another Razakar, an associate of Kenan Uddin Sarkar informed the Pakistani army. The Pakistani army took the hostage Hindus to Akhira, 100 metres from south of Baraihat. It was about 11 A.M. The Hindus were made to stand in a row beside a pond, the men in one line and the women and children in another. They were burst fired from machine guns. A few children and teenagers who were survived the burst fire, were bayonetted to death. According to eye witness accounts, after gunning down the men, the Pakistani soldiers turned their attention to the females, and brutally gang raped them at that spot.

Aftermath
According to the most conservative reports, the casualty figure is 85. Eight local Muslims, who had witnessed the massacre were also killed later. According to other version, around 125 Hindus died in the massacre. 

After the victory in the Liberation War, the local people executed Kenan Uddin Sarkar by the method of Jabiha.

843428053a.d:
Coming from Brahma's Kamandalu, Pushkara Raja resides in different rivers, along with 3.5 crore tirthas, following the Sankranti of Guru, for twelve days at the beginning of the Sankranti (ādya puṣkaram) and at the end of the year (preceding transition to the next rāśī, antya puṣkaram), and for two muhurtas during mid-day, every day, during the entire year.
As Guru is about to leave vr̥ṣabhaḥ, puṣkararāja's residence in the narmadā river draws to a close.

844d96b48a.s:
𑌨𑌾𑌰𑌦 𑌉𑌵𑌾𑌚---  
𑌶𑍃𑌣𑍁 𑌬𑍍𑌰𑌹𑍍𑌮𑌨𑍍𑌪𑍍𑌰𑌵𑌕𑍍𑌷𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌮𑌿 𑌮𑌾𑌹𑌾𑌤𑍍𑌮𑍍𑌯𑌂 𑌪𑌾𑌪𑌨𑌾𑌶𑌨𑌮𑍍।  
𑌅𑌕𑍍𑌷𑌯𑌾𑌯𑌾 𑌨𑌵𑌮𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌸𑍍𑌤𑍁 𑌯𑌦𑍍𑌗𑍋𑌪𑍍𑌯𑌂 𑌚 𑌤𑍍𑌰𑌿𑌵𑌿𑌷𑍍𑌟𑌪𑍇॥௧॥  
𑌤𑌦𑌹𑌂 𑌤𑍇 𑌸𑌮𑌗𑍍𑌰𑌂 𑌚 𑌕𑌥𑌯𑌿𑌷𑍍𑌯𑍇 𑌤𑌪𑍋𑌧𑌨।  
𑌕𑌾𑌰𑍍𑌤𑌿𑌕𑌸𑍍𑌯 𑌤𑍁 𑌶𑍁𑌕𑍍𑌲𑌸𑍍𑌯 𑌪𑌕𑍍𑌷𑌸𑍍𑌯 𑌨𑌵𑌮𑍀𑌤𑌿𑌥𑌿𑌃॥௨॥  
𑌅𑌕𑍍𑌷𑌯𑌾 𑌸𑌾 𑌤𑍁 𑌸𑌮𑍍𑌪𑍍𑌰𑍋𑌕𑍍𑌤𑌾 𑌵𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌸𑌾𑌦𑍍𑌯𑍈𑌰𑍍𑌮𑍁𑌨𑌿𑌪𑍁𑌙𑍍𑌗𑌵𑍈𑌃।  
𑌤𑌸𑍍𑌮𑌾𑌤𑍍𑌤𑍁 𑌕𑌰𑌣𑌂 𑌯𑌤𑍍𑌸𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌤𑍍𑌤𑌚𑍍𑌛𑍃𑌣𑍁𑌧𑍍𑌵𑌂 𑌹𑌰𑌿𑌪𑍍𑌰𑌿𑌯𑌮𑍍॥௩॥  
𑌬𑍍𑌰𑌾𑌹𑍍𑌮𑍇 𑌮𑍁𑌹𑍂𑌰𑍍𑌤𑍇 𑌚𑍋𑌤𑍍𑌥𑌾𑌯 𑌚𑌿𑌨𑍍𑌤𑌯𑍇𑌦𑌾𑌤𑍍𑌮𑌨𑍋 𑌹𑌿𑌤𑌮𑍍।  
𑌕𑍃𑌤𑍍𑌵𑌾 𑌨𑌿𑌮𑌿𑌤𑍍𑌤𑌕𑌂 𑌕𑌰𑍍𑌮 𑌪𑍂𑌜𑌯𑍇𑌦𑌿𑌷𑍍𑌟𑌦𑍇𑌵𑌤𑌾𑌃॥௪॥  
𑌵𑌿𑌷𑍍𑌣𑍁𑌪𑍂𑌜𑌾𑌂 𑌵𑌿𑌧𑌾𑌯𑌾𑌽𑌽𑌦𑍌 𑌤𑌥𑌾 𑌪𑌞𑍍𑌚𑍋𑌪𑌚𑌾𑌰𑌕𑍈𑌃।  
𑌪𑍍𑌰𑌦𑌦𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌤𑍍𑌤𑌤𑍍𑌰 𑌨𑍈𑌵𑍇𑌦𑍍𑌯𑌂 𑌪𑌕𑍍𑌵𑌾𑌨𑍍𑌨𑌂 𑌸𑌲𑌵𑌙𑍍𑌗𑌕𑌮𑍍॥௫॥  
𑌜𑍀𑌰𑌕𑌂 𑌨𑌾𑌗𑌰𑌂 𑌕𑍃𑌷𑍍𑌣𑌮𑌰𑌿𑌚𑌂 𑌦𑌾𑌡𑌿𑌮𑌂 𑌤𑌥𑌾।  
𑌨𑌾𑌰𑌿𑌕𑍇𑌲𑌫𑌲𑌂 𑌚𑌾𑌨𑍍𑌯𑌤𑍍𑌕𑍂𑌷𑍍𑌮𑌾𑌣𑍍𑌡𑌕𑌾𑌞𑍍𑌚𑌨𑍀𑌯𑍁𑌤𑌮𑍍॥௬॥  
𑌸𑌙𑍍𑌕𑌲𑍍𑌪𑍍𑌯 𑌦𑌦𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌚𑍍𑌛𑍍𑌰𑍀𑌕𑍃𑌷𑍍𑌣𑌃 𑌪𑍍𑌰𑍀𑌯𑌤𑌾𑌮𑌿𑌤𑌿 𑌚𑌾𑌕𑍍𑌷𑌯𑌃।  
𑌸𑍍𑌵𑌶𑌕𑍍𑌤𑍍𑌯𑌾 𑌤𑍋𑌷𑌯𑍇𑌦𑍍𑌵𑌿𑌪𑍍𑌰𑌾𑌨𑍍𑌨𑌮𑌸𑍍𑌕𑌾𑌰𑍇𑌣 𑌵𑌾 𑌪𑍁𑌨𑌃॥௭॥  
𑌸𑍂𑌰𑍍𑌯𑌗𑍍𑌰𑌹𑍇 𑌕𑍁𑌰𑍁𑌕𑍍𑌷𑍇𑌤𑍍𑌰𑍇 𑌤𑍁𑌲𑌾𑌦𑌾𑌨𑌸𑍍𑌯 𑌯𑌤𑍍𑌫𑌲𑌮𑍍।  
𑌤𑌤𑍍𑌫𑌲𑌂 𑌲𑌭𑌤𑍇 𑌮𑌰𑍍𑌤𑍍𑌯𑌸𑍍𑌤𑌸𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌂 𑌕𑍂𑌷𑍍𑌮𑌾𑌣𑍍𑌡𑌦𑌾𑌨𑌤𑌃॥௮॥  
𑌮𑌹𑌾𑌪𑌾𑌤𑌕𑌯𑍁𑌕𑍍𑌤𑍋𑌽𑌪𑌿 𑌤𑌦𑍍𑌯𑍁𑌕𑍍𑌤𑍋 𑌚𑍋𑌪𑌪𑌾𑌤𑌕𑍈𑌃।  
𑌨𑌰𑍋 𑌵𑌿𑌶𑍁𑌦𑍍𑌧𑌮𑍁𑌕𑍍𑌤𑍋 𑌹𑌿 𑌯𑌮𑌲𑍋𑌕𑌂 𑌨 𑌪𑌶𑍍𑌯𑌤𑌿॥௯॥  
𑌕𑍂𑌷𑍍𑌮𑌾𑌣𑍍𑌡𑌦𑌾𑌨𑌕𑌰𑍍𑌤𑌾𑌰𑌃 𑌸𑌰𑍍𑌵𑌲𑍋𑌕𑌾𑌨𑍍𑌵𑍍𑌰𑌜𑌨𑍍𑌤𑌿 𑌵𑍈।  
𑌸𑍍𑌵𑍇𑌚𑍍𑌛𑌯𑌾 𑌪𑌰𑍍𑌯𑌟𑌨𑍍𑌤𑌶𑍍𑌚 𑌨𑌾𑌨𑌾𑌭𑍋𑌗𑌰𑌤𑌾 𑌦𑍍𑌵𑌿𑌜॥௧௦॥  
𑌶𑍌𑌨𑌕 𑌉𑌵𑌾𑌚---  
𑌭𑍂𑌲𑍋𑌕𑍇 𑌕𑍇𑌨 𑌦𑌤𑍍𑌤𑌂 𑌹𑌿 𑌵𑌦 𑌮𑌹𑍍𑌯𑌂 𑌮𑍁𑌨𑍀𑌶𑍍𑌵𑌰।  
𑌦𑌾𑌨𑌂 𑌕𑍂𑌷𑍍𑌮𑌾𑌣𑍍𑌡𑌕𑌮𑌯𑌂 𑌯𑍇𑌨 𑌕𑍌𑌤𑍂𑌹𑌲𑌂 𑌹𑌿 𑌮𑍇॥௧௧॥  
𑌨𑌾𑌰𑌦 𑌉𑌵𑌾𑌚---  
𑌅𑌨𑍍𑌤𑌰𑍍𑌵𑍇𑌦𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌂 𑌮𑌹𑌾𑌗𑍍𑌰𑌾𑌮𑍋 𑌯𑌾𑌮𑍁𑌨𑌸𑍍𑌯 𑌗𑌿𑌰𑍇𑌰𑌧𑌃।  
𑌤𑌤𑍍𑌰 𑌸𑍁𑌬𑍍𑌰𑌾𑌹𑍍𑌮𑌣𑍋 𑌰𑌾𑌮𑌶𑌰𑍍𑌮𑌾𑌽𑌸𑍌 𑌲𑍋𑌕𑌵𑌿𑌶𑍍𑌰𑍁𑌤𑌃॥௧௨॥  
𑌤𑍇𑌨𑌾𑌤𑍍𑌯𑌨𑍍𑌤𑌧𑌨𑌂 𑌸𑌮𑍍𑌯𑌗𑌰𑍍𑌜𑌿𑌤𑌂 𑌪𑍍𑌰𑌚𑍁𑌰𑌂 𑌕𑌿𑌲।  
𑌪𑍁𑌣𑍍𑌯𑌕𑌾𑌰𑍍𑌯𑌪𑌰𑍋𑌦𑌾𑌤𑌾 𑌵𑌾𑌰𑍍𑌦𑍍𑌧𑌕𑍍𑌯𑌂 𑌸𑌮𑍁𑌪𑌾𑌗𑌤𑌃॥௧௩॥  
𑌤𑌸𑍍𑌯 𑌪𑍁𑌤𑍍𑌰𑍌 𑌤𑍁 𑌸𑌞𑍍𑌜𑌾𑌤𑍌 𑌨𑌾𑌮𑍍𑌨𑌾 𑌕𑍃𑌷𑍍𑌣𑌧𑌨𑌞𑍍𑌜𑌯𑍌।  
𑌤𑌯𑍋𑌰𑍍𑌮𑍂𑌰𑍍𑌦𑍍𑌧𑌵𑌹𑌂 𑌦𑌤𑍍𑌤𑍍𑌵𑌾 𑌜𑌗𑌾𑌮 𑌤𑌪𑌸𑍇 𑌵𑌨𑌮𑍍॥௧௪॥  
𑌤𑌪𑌃 𑌕𑍍𑌲𑌿𑌷𑍍𑌟𑌶𑌰𑍀𑌰𑍋𑌽𑌸𑍌 𑌵𑌾𑌸𑍁𑌦𑍇𑌵𑌮𑌨𑌃 𑌸𑌦𑌾।  
𑌪𑍍𑌰𑌾𑌪𑍍𑌤𑌵𑌾𑌨𑍍𑌵𑍈𑌷𑍍𑌣𑌵𑌂 𑌸𑍍𑌥𑌾𑌨𑌂 𑌯𑌤𑍍𑌰 𑌗𑌤𑍍𑌵𑌾 𑌨 𑌶𑍋𑌚𑌤𑌿॥௧௫॥  
𑌤𑌤𑌸𑍍𑌤𑌸𑍍𑌯 𑌸𑍁𑌤𑍌 𑌤𑍌 𑌤𑍁 𑌕𑌾𑌲𑍇 𑌤𑌰𑍁𑌣𑌾𑌤𑌾𑌂 𑌗𑌤𑍌।  
𑌵𑌾𑌰𑌸𑍍𑌤𑍍𑌰𑍀𑌰𑌤𑌿𑌸𑌂𑌸𑌕𑍍𑌤𑍌 𑌮𑌦𑍍𑌯𑌪𑌾𑌨𑌰𑌤𑍌 𑌸𑌦𑌾॥௧௬॥  
𑌨 𑌶𑍃𑌣𑍍𑌵𑌤𑍇 𑌵𑌚𑌃 𑌪𑍂𑌰𑍍𑌵𑌂 𑌵𑍃𑌦𑍍𑌧𑌾𑌨𑌾𑌂 𑌤𑌤𑍍𑌰 𑌤𑌾𑌵𑍁𑌭𑍌।  
𑌪𑌰𑌸𑍍𑌤𑍍𑌰𑌾𑌭𑍍𑌯𑌃 𑌪𑍍𑌰𑌦𑌦𑌤𑍁𑌃 𑌸𑌹𑌸𑍍𑌰𑌂 𑌚 𑌶𑌤𑌂 𑌤𑌥𑌾॥௧௭॥  
𑌏𑌵𑌂 𑌦𑍍𑌰𑌵𑍍𑌯𑌂 𑌕𑍍𑌷𑌯𑌂 𑌨𑍀𑌤𑌂 𑌤𑌾𑌭𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌂 𑌕𑍍𑌷𑌣𑌸𑍁𑌖𑌾𑌯 𑌵𑍈  
𑌮𑌲𑍍𑌲𑍌 𑌚𑌾𑌣𑍂𑌰𑌶𑍈𑌲𑍂𑌷𑍌 𑌵𑍇𑌶𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌦𑍍𑌯𑍁𑌤𑌪𑍍𑌰𑌿𑌯𑌾𑌵𑍁𑌭𑍌॥௧௮॥  
𑌅𑌪𑌾𑌤𑍍𑌰𑍇 𑌤𑌦𑍍𑌧𑌨𑌂 𑌦𑌤𑍍𑌤𑌂 𑌭𑍁𑌵𑌿 𑌬𑍀𑌜𑌮𑌿𑌵𑍋𑌷𑌰𑍇।  
𑌦𑍍𑌰𑌵𑍍𑌯𑌕𑍍𑌷𑌯𑌾𑌦𑍁𑌭𑍌 𑌭𑍂𑌤𑍌 𑌚𑍌𑌰𑌮𑌾𑌰𑍍𑌗𑌾𑌨𑍁𑌸𑌾𑌰𑌿𑌣𑍌॥௧௯॥  
𑌰𑌾𑌤𑍍𑌰𑍌 𑌤𑍁 𑌕𑍋𑌟𑌪𑌾𑌲𑍇𑌨 𑌧𑍃𑌤𑌾 𑌰𑌾𑌜𑍍𑌞𑌾 𑌚 𑌵𑌾𑌸𑌿𑌤𑍌।  
𑌵𑌨𑌂 𑌗𑌤𑍌 𑌤𑍁 𑌤𑍌 𑌸𑌾𑌰𑍍𑌧𑌮𑌧𑌰𑍍𑌮𑌨𑌿𑌰𑌤𑍌 𑌦𑍍𑌵𑌿𑌜𑍌॥௨௦॥  
𑌮𑌾𑌂𑌸𑌾𑌹𑌾𑌰𑌿𑌣𑍌 𑌸𑌞𑍍𑌜𑌾𑌤𑍌 𑌸𑌿𑌂𑌹𑌾𑌨𑍍𑌮𑍃𑌤𑍍𑌯𑍁𑌮𑍁𑌪𑌾𑌗𑌤𑍌।  
𑌏𑌕𑌸𑍍𑌮𑌿𑌨𑍍𑌦𑌿𑌵𑌸𑍇 𑌬𑍍𑌰𑌹𑍍𑌮𑌨𑍍𑌮𑍃𑌤𑍌 𑌯𑌮𑌪𑍁𑌰𑌂 𑌗𑌤𑍌॥௨௧॥  
𑌯𑌮𑌦𑍂𑌤𑍌 𑌤𑌦𑌾 𑌵𑌾𑌕𑍍𑌯𑌂 𑌕𑌾 𑌶𑌾𑌸𑍍𑌤𑌿𑌃 𑌕𑍍𑌰𑌿𑌯𑌤𑍇 𑌵𑌿𑌭𑍋।  
𑌕𑌿𑌙𑍍𑌕𑌰𑌸𑍍𑌯 𑌵𑌚𑌃 𑌶𑍍𑌰𑍁𑌤𑍍𑌵𑌾 𑌤𑌦𑌾 𑌵𑍈𑌵𑌸𑍍𑌵𑌤𑍋 𑌯𑌮𑌃॥௨௨॥  
𑌚𑌿𑌤𑍍𑌰𑌗𑍁𑌪𑍍𑌤𑌲𑍇𑌖𑌨𑍀𑌯𑌂 𑌨𑌰𑌾𑌣𑌾𑌂 𑌚 𑌶𑍁𑌭𑌾𑌶𑍁𑌭𑌮𑍍।  
𑌏𑌕𑌤𑍍𑌰 𑌕𑍍𑌰𑍋𑌧𑌤𑌾𑌮𑍍𑌰𑌾𑌕𑍍𑌷𑌃 𑌏𑌤𑍌 𑌕𑍁𑌤𑍍𑌰 𑌕𑍍𑌷𑌿𑌪𑌾𑌮𑍍𑌯𑌹𑌮𑍍॥௨௩॥  
𑌚𑌿𑌤𑍍𑌰𑌗𑍁𑌪𑍍𑌤𑍋𑌽𑌬𑍍𑌰𑌵𑍀𑌦𑍍𑌵𑌾𑌕𑍍𑌯𑌂 𑌕𑌿𑌙𑍍𑌕𑌰𑌾𑌨𑍍𑌶𑍂𑌲𑌧𑌾𑌰𑌿𑌣𑌃।  
𑌏𑌕𑌶𑍍𑌚 𑌨𑍀𑌯𑌤𑌾𑌂 𑌸𑍍𑌵𑌰𑍍𑌗𑍇 𑌯𑌤𑍍𑌰 𑌭𑍋𑌗𑌶𑍍𑌚 𑌶𑌾𑌶𑍍𑌵𑌤𑌾𑌃॥௨௪॥  
𑌅𑌪𑌰𑍋 𑌕𑍍𑌷𑌿𑌪𑍍𑌯𑌤𑌾𑌂 𑌦𑍂𑌤𑌾 𑌨𑌰𑌕𑍇 𑌯𑌾𑌤𑌨𑌾𑌕𑍁𑌲𑍇।  
𑌚𑌿𑌤𑍍𑌰𑌗𑍁𑌪𑍍𑌤𑌵𑌚𑌃 𑌶𑍍𑌰𑍁𑌤𑍍𑌵𑌾 𑌤𑌦𑌾 𑌦𑍂𑌤𑌃 𑌪𑍍𑌰𑌿𑌯𑌂𑌵𑌦𑌃॥௨௫॥  
𑌨𑍀𑌤𑍍𑌵𑌾 𑌧𑌨𑌞𑍍𑌜𑌯𑌂 𑌤𑍁𑌷𑍍𑌟𑌃 𑌸𑍍𑌵𑌰𑍍𑌗𑌮𑌾𑌰𑍍𑌗𑌮𑍁𑌪𑌾𑌗𑌤𑌃।  
𑌅𑌨𑍍𑌯𑌸𑍍𑌤𑍁 𑌪𑌾𑌪𑌕𑌰𑍍𑌮𑌾𑌣𑌂 𑌗𑍃𑌹𑍀𑌤𑍍𑌵𑌾 𑌕𑍃𑌷𑍍𑌣𑌶𑌰𑍍𑌮𑌕𑌮𑍍॥௨௬॥  
𑌨𑌰𑌕𑍇𑌽𑌪𑌾𑌤𑌯𑌤𑍍𑌕𑍍𑌰𑍁𑌦𑍍𑌧𑍋 𑌭𑍁𑌙𑍍𑌕𑍍𑌷𑍍𑌵 𑌕𑌰𑍍𑌮𑌕𑍃𑌤𑌂 𑌦𑍍𑌵𑌿𑌜।  
𑌧𑌨𑌞𑍍𑌜𑌯𑍋 𑌵𑍍𑌰𑌜𑌨𑍍𑌮𑌾𑌰𑍍𑌗𑍇 𑌪𑌶𑍍𑌯𑌨𑍍𑌵𑍈𑌚𑌿𑌤𑍍𑌰𑍍𑌯𑌮𑌾𑌪𑍍𑌤𑌵𑌾𑌨𑍍॥௨௭॥  
𑌅𑌪𑍍𑌸𑌰𑌾𑌶𑍍𑌚 𑌤𑌦𑌾𑌗𑌤𑍍𑌯 𑌉𑌰𑍍𑌵𑌶𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌦𑍍𑌯𑌾 𑌮𑌹𑌾𑌮𑍁𑌨𑍇।  
𑌪𑌾𑌰𑌿𑌜𑌾𑌤𑌕𑍃𑌤𑌾𑌂 𑌮𑌾𑌲𑌾𑌂 𑌶𑌿𑌰𑌸𑌿 𑌪𑍍𑌰𑌾𑌕𑍍𑌷𑌿𑌪𑌨𑍍𑌮𑍁𑌦𑌾॥௨௮॥  
𑌇𑌤𑌿 𑌦𑍃𑌷𑍍𑌟𑍍𑌵𑌾 𑌤𑌦𑌾𑌶𑍍𑌚𑌰𑍍𑌯𑌂 𑌸𑍍𑌵𑌰𑍍𑌗𑌮𑌾𑌰𑍍𑌗𑌸𑍍𑌯 𑌶𑍌𑌨𑌕।  
𑌪𑍃𑌷𑍍𑌟𑌵𑌾𑌨𑍍 𑌯𑌮𑌦𑍂𑌤𑌂 𑌚 𑌤𑌦𑌾 𑌸𑌕𑌰𑍁𑌣𑌂 𑌵𑌚𑌃॥௨௯॥  
𑌧𑌨𑌞𑍍𑌜𑌯 𑌉𑌵𑌾𑌚---  
𑌏𑌕𑌾 𑌮𑌾𑌤𑌾 𑌪𑌿𑌤𑌾 𑌚𑍈𑌕𑌸𑍍𑌤𑌾𑌭𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌂 𑌜𑌾𑌤𑍌 𑌸𑌹𑍋𑌦𑌰𑍌।  
𑌪𑌾𑌪𑌮𑍇𑌵 𑌕𑍃𑌤𑌂 𑌤𑌾𑌭𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌂 𑌨 𑌵𑌾𑌰𑍍𑌤𑌾 𑌪𑍁𑌣𑍍𑌯𑌕𑌰𑍍𑌮𑌣𑌃॥௩௦॥  
𑌏𑌕𑌸𑍍𑌮𑌿𑌨𑍍𑌦𑌿𑌵𑌸𑍇 𑌦𑍂𑌤 𑌮𑍃𑌤𑍌 𑌯𑌮𑌪𑍁𑌰𑍀𑌂 𑌗𑌤𑍌।  
𑌕𑌥𑌂 𑌸 𑌨𑌰𑌕𑍇 𑌕𑍍𑌷𑌿𑌪𑍍𑌤𑍋 𑌮𑌮 𑌜𑍍𑌯𑍇𑌷𑍍𑌠𑌃 𑌪𑍍𑌰𑌿𑌯𑌂𑌵𑌦॥௩௧॥  
𑌮𑌮 𑌭𑌾𑌵𑍀 𑌕𑌥𑌂 𑌨𑌾𑌥 𑌸𑌂𑌶𑌯𑍋𑌽𑌸𑍍𑌤𑌿 𑌮𑌹𑌾𑌨𑍍𑌮𑌮।  
𑌯𑌮𑌦𑍂𑌤 𑌉𑌵𑌾𑌚---  
𑌸𑍍𑌵𑌸𑌾 𑌮𑌾𑌤𑌾 𑌪𑌿𑌤𑌾 𑌭𑍍𑌰𑌾𑌤𑌾 𑌪𑌿𑌤𑍃𑌵𑍍𑌯𑌶𑍍𑌚 𑌧𑌨𑌞𑍍𑌜𑌯।  
𑌅𑌦𑍃𑌷𑍍𑌟𑌕𑌰𑍍𑌮𑌜𑌾 𑌸𑌂𑌜𑍍𑌞𑌾 𑌜𑌨𑍍𑌮𑌕𑌰𑍍𑌮𑍋𑌪𑌭𑍁𑌕𑍍𑌤𑌯𑍇॥௩௨॥  
𑌯𑌥𑌾 𑌕𑌨𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌗𑌤𑍇 𑌸𑍂𑌰𑍍𑌯𑍇 𑌶𑍍𑌵𑌶𑍁𑌨𑍀𑌨𑌾𑌂 𑌸𑌮𑌾𑌗𑌮𑌃।  
𑌪𑍁𑌤𑍍𑌰𑌭𑍍𑌰𑌾𑌤𑍃𑌪𑌿𑌤𑍄𑌣𑌾𑌂 𑌚 𑌤𑌥𑌾 𑌭𑌵𑌤𑌿 𑌸𑌙𑍍𑌗𑌮𑌃॥௩௩॥  
𑌤𑌸𑍍𑌮𑌾𑌚𑍍𑌚𑌿𑌨𑍍𑌤𑌾 𑌨 𑌕𑌰𑍍𑌤𑌵𑍍𑌯𑌾 𑌵𑍍𑌰𑌜 𑌮𑌾𑌰𑍍𑌗 𑌪𑍁𑌰𑌸𑍍𑌯 𑌵𑍈।  
𑌪𑍁𑌣𑍍𑌯𑌵𑌾𑌂𑌸𑍍𑌤𑍍𑌵𑌂 𑌸𑍁𑌕𑍃𑌤𑌿𑌨𑌾𑌂 𑌲𑍋𑌕𑌂 𑌯𑌾𑌸𑌿 𑌨𑌮𑍋𑌽𑌸𑍍𑌤𑍁 𑌤𑍇॥௩௪॥  
𑌕𑍇𑌨 𑌪𑍁𑌣𑍍𑌯𑍇𑌨 𑌮𑌾𑌂 𑌦𑍂𑌤 𑌨𑌯𑌸𑌿 𑌤𑍍𑌵𑌂 𑌤𑍍𑌰𑌿𑌵𑌿𑌷𑍍𑌟𑌪𑌮𑍍।  
𑌪𑌾𑌪𑌿𑌷𑍍𑌠𑌾 𑌮𑌤𑍍𑌪𑌰𑍋 𑌨𑌾𑌨𑍍𑌯𑍋 𑌭𑌵𑌿𑌷𑍍𑌯𑌤𑌿 𑌧𑌰𑌾𑌤𑌲𑍇॥௩௫॥  
𑌤𑌸𑍍𑌯 𑌤𑌦𑍍𑌵𑌚𑌨𑌂 𑌶𑍍𑌰𑍁𑌤𑍍𑌵𑌾 𑌯𑌮𑌦𑍂𑌤𑍋𑌽𑌬𑍍𑌰𑌵𑍀𑌦𑍍𑌵𑌚𑌃।  
𑌪𑌾𑌠𑌕𑌸𑍍𑌯 𑌪𑍍𑌰𑌸𑌙𑍍𑌗𑍇𑌨 𑌗𑌤𑌸𑍍𑌤𑍍𑌵𑌂 𑌯𑌮𑍁𑌨𑌾𑌂 𑌕𑌿𑌲।  
𑌵𑌾𑌸𑌸𑍀 𑌚 𑌗𑍁𑌰𑍋𑌰𑍍𑌗𑍃𑌹𑍍𑌯 𑌕𑍁𑌶𑌾𑌂𑌶𑍍𑌚 𑌸𑌮𑌿𑌧𑌸𑍍𑌤𑌥𑌾॥௩௬॥  
𑌆𑌚𑌾𑌰𑍍𑌯𑌸𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌜𑍍𑌞𑌯𑌾 𑌸𑍍𑌨𑌾𑌨𑌮𑍂𑌰𑍍𑌜𑍇 𑌪𑍍𑌰𑌾𑌤𑌃 𑌕𑍃𑌤𑌂 𑌤𑍍𑌰𑍍𑌯𑌹𑌮𑍍।  
𑌨𑌿𑌯𑌮𑌂 𑌯𑌤𑍍𑌕𑍃𑌤𑌂 𑌤𑌤𑍍𑌰 𑌸𑌞𑍍𑌜𑌾𑌤𑌸𑍍𑌤𑍁 𑌮𑌹𑌤𑍍𑌫𑌲𑌮𑍍॥௩௭॥  
𑌏𑌕𑍇𑌨 𑌮𑌜𑍍𑌜𑍇𑌨𑌨𑌾𑌶𑍁 𑌪𑌾𑌪𑌾𑌨𑍍𑌮𑍁𑌕𑍍𑌤𑍋𑌽𑌸𑌿 𑌜𑌨𑍍𑌮𑌨𑌃।  
𑌮𑌜𑍍𑌜𑌨𑍇𑌨 𑌦𑍍𑌵𑌿𑌤𑍀𑌯𑍇𑌨 𑌅𑌕𑍍𑌷𑌯𑌂 𑌸𑍍𑌵𑌰𑍍𑌗𑌮𑌾𑌪𑍍𑌨𑍁𑌹𑌿॥௩௮॥  
𑌨𑌰𑌕𑍇 𑌚 𑌤𑌵 𑌭𑍍𑌰𑌾𑌤𑌾 𑌸𑌹𑌤𑌾𑌂 𑌯𑌮𑌯𑌾𑌤𑌨𑌾𑌮𑍍।  
𑌇𑌤𑌿 𑌶𑍍𑌰𑍁𑌤𑍍𑌵𑌾 𑌵𑌚𑌸𑍍𑌤𑌸𑍍𑌯 𑌭𑍍𑌰𑌾𑌤𑍃𑌗𑍌𑌰𑌵𑌯𑌨𑍍𑌤𑍍𑌰𑌿𑌤𑌃॥௩௯॥  
𑌦𑍇𑌵𑌦𑍂𑌤 𑌪𑍍𑌰𑌣𑌮𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌹𑌂 𑌮𑍈𑌤𑍍𑌰𑍀𑌂 𑌸𑌾𑌪𑍍𑌤𑌪𑌦𑍀𑌂 𑌸𑍍𑌮𑌰𑌨𑍍।  
𑌨𑌿𑌰𑍍𑌗𑌮𑍋 𑌨𑌰𑌕𑌾𑌦𑍍 𑌦𑍂𑌤 𑌭𑍍𑌰𑌾𑌤𑍁𑌰𑍍𑌮𑍇 𑌜𑌾𑌯𑌤𑍇 𑌕𑌥𑌮𑍍॥௪௦॥  
𑌯𑌥𑌾𑌽𑌹𑌂 𑌭𑍍𑌰𑌾𑌤𑍃𑌸𑌙𑍍𑌗𑍇𑌨 𑌸𑍍𑌵𑌰𑍍𑌗𑌂 𑌯𑌾𑌮𑌿 𑌪𑍍𑌰𑌿𑌯𑌂𑌵𑌦।  
𑌨 𑌹𑌿 𑌭𑍍𑌰𑌾𑌤𑍃𑌸𑌮𑍋 𑌬𑌨𑍍𑌧𑍁𑌰𑍍𑌨 𑌹𑌿 𑌭𑍍𑌰𑌾𑌤𑍃𑌸𑌮𑌃 𑌸𑌖𑌾॥௪௧॥  
𑌨 𑌹𑌿 𑌭𑍍𑌰𑌾𑌤𑍃𑌸𑌮𑍋 𑌤𑍍𑌰𑌾𑌤𑌾 𑌮𑌾𑌤𑍃𑌜𑌾𑌤𑌂 𑌵𑌿𑌶𑍇𑌷𑌤𑌃।  
𑌸𑍍𑌵𑌰𑍍𑌗𑌂 𑌨𑍇𑌚𑍍𑌛𑍇 𑌵𑌿𑌨𑌾 𑌤𑍇𑌨 𑌤𑌤𑍍𑌰 𑌮𑍇 𑌕𑌾𑌰𑍍𑌯𑌨𑌿𑌰𑍍𑌵𑍃𑌤𑌿𑌃॥௪௨॥  
𑌯𑌥𑌾 𑌭𑍍𑌰𑌾𑌤𑌾 𑌸𑌮𑍋 𑌯𑍋𑌗𑌸𑍍𑌤𑌮𑍁𑌪𑌾𑌯𑌂 𑌵𑌦𑌸𑍍𑌵 𑌮𑍇।  
𑌇𑌤𑌿 𑌶𑍍𑌰𑍁𑌤𑍍𑌵𑌾 𑌵𑌚𑌸𑍍𑌤𑌸𑍍𑌯 𑌦𑍇𑌵𑌦𑍂𑌤𑍋𑌽𑌬𑍍𑌰𑌵𑍀𑌤𑍍𑌤𑌤𑌃॥௪௩॥  
𑌪𑍂𑌰𑍍𑌵𑌜𑌨𑍍𑌮𑌕𑍃𑌤𑌂 𑌪𑍁𑌣𑍍𑌯𑌂 𑌤𑌦𑍍𑌵𑌦𑌾𑌮𑌿 𑌧𑌨𑌞𑍍𑌜𑌯।  
𑌦𑌾𑌨𑌂 𑌨𑌵𑌮𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌂 𑌕𑍂𑌷𑍍𑌮𑌾𑌣𑍍𑌡𑌸𑍍𑌯𑍋𑌰𑍍𑌜𑍇𑌶𑍁𑌕𑍍𑌲𑌤𑌿𑌥𑍌 𑌦𑌿𑌨𑍇॥௪௪॥  
𑌸𑌹𑌿𑌰𑌣𑍍𑌯𑌂 𑌤𑍍𑌵𑌯𑌾 𑌦𑌤𑍍𑌤𑌂 𑌸𑌰𑌤𑍍𑌨𑌂 𑌚 𑌸𑌵𑌸𑍍𑌤𑍍𑌰𑌕𑌮𑍍।  
𑌦𑍇𑌹𑌿 𑌪𑍁𑌣𑍍𑌯𑌂 𑌚 𑌤𑍍𑌵𑌂 𑌭𑍍𑌰𑌾𑌤𑍍𑌰𑍇 𑌦𑍁𑌷𑍍𑌪𑍍𑌰𑌾𑌪𑍍𑌯𑌂 𑌸𑍍𑌵𑌰𑍍𑌗𑌿𑌣𑌾𑌮𑌪𑌿॥௪௫॥  
𑌇𑌤𑌿 𑌶𑍍𑌰𑍁𑌤𑍍𑌵𑌾 𑌵𑌚𑌸𑍍𑌤𑌸𑍍𑌯 𑌦𑍇𑌵𑌦𑍂𑌤𑌸𑍍𑌯 𑌸𑌾𑌦𑌰𑌮𑍍।  
𑌦𑌦𑍌 𑌭𑍍𑌰𑌾𑌤𑍍𑌰𑍇 𑌚 𑌕𑍂𑌷𑍍𑌮𑌾𑌣𑍍𑌡𑌦𑌾𑌨𑌪𑍁𑌣𑍍𑌯𑌂 𑌧𑌨𑌞𑍍𑌜𑌯𑌃॥௪௬॥  
𑌪𑍁𑌣𑍍𑌯𑌦𑌾𑌨𑍇𑌨 𑌕𑍃𑌷𑍍𑌣𑍋𑌽𑌪𑌿 𑌨𑌰𑌕𑌾𑌦𑌾𑌗𑌤𑌸𑍍𑌤𑌦𑌾।  
𑌭𑍍𑌰𑌾𑌤𑍍𑌰𑌾 𑌸𑌹 𑌦𑍍𑌵𑌿𑌜𑌵𑌰𑌃 𑌪𑍍𑌰𑌾𑌪𑍍𑌤𑌵𑌾𑌨𑍍 𑌵𑍈𑌷𑍍𑌣𑌵𑌂 𑌪𑌦𑌮𑍍॥௪௭॥  
𑌭𑍋𑌗𑍋𑌪𑌭𑍋𑌗𑌸𑌮𑍍𑌪𑌨𑍍𑌨𑍌 𑌯𑌮𑌦𑍂𑌤𑌵𑌿𑌵𑌰𑍍𑌜𑌿𑌤𑍌।  
𑌅𑌦𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌪𑌿 𑌤𑍌 𑌦𑍍𑌵𑌿𑌜𑌵𑌰𑍌 𑌪𑍁𑌣𑍍𑌯𑌶𑍀𑌲𑌸𑍁𑌶𑍀𑌲𑌕𑍌॥௪௮॥  
𑌕𑍃𑌷𑍍𑌣𑌭𑌕𑍍𑌤𑌾𑌵𑌭𑍂𑌤𑌾𑌂 𑌵𑍈 𑌕𑍃𑌷𑍍𑌣𑌾𑌰𑌾𑌧𑌨𑌤𑌤𑍍𑌪𑌰𑍌।  
𑌨𑌵𑌮𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌂 𑌕𑍃𑌷𑍍𑌣𑌮𑍁𑌦𑍍𑌦𑌿𑌶𑍍𑌯 𑌶𑍁𑌕𑍍𑌲𑌪𑌕𑍍𑌷𑍇 𑌵𑌿𑌚𑌕𑍍𑌷𑌣𑍈𑌃॥௪௯॥  
𑌕𑌾𑌰𑍍𑌤𑌿𑌕𑍇 𑌮𑌾𑌸𑌿 𑌕𑍂𑌷𑍍𑌮𑌾𑌣𑍍𑌡𑌂 𑌸𑌹𑌿𑌰𑌣𑍍𑌯𑌂 𑌸𑌵𑌸𑍍𑌤𑍍𑌰𑌕𑌮𑍍।  
𑌕𑍂𑌷𑍍𑌮𑌾𑌣𑍍𑌡𑌸𑍍𑌯 𑌚 𑌦𑌾𑌨𑍇𑌨 𑌤𑌾𑌰𑍍𑌯𑌨𑍍𑌤𑍇 𑌕𑍋𑌟𑌿𑌪𑍂𑌰𑍁𑌷𑌾𑌃॥௫௦॥  
𑌏𑌤𑌤𑍍𑌤𑍇 𑌕𑌥𑌿𑌤𑌂 𑌵𑌿𑌪𑍍𑌰 𑌕𑌾𑌰𑍍𑌤𑌿𑌕𑌨𑌵𑌮𑍀𑌵𑍍𑌰𑌤𑌮𑍍।  
𑌕𑍂𑌷𑍍𑌮𑌾𑌣𑍍𑌡𑌦𑌾𑌨𑌮𑌾𑌹𑌾𑌤𑍍𑌮𑍍𑌯𑌂 𑌯𑌦𑍍𑌗𑍀𑌤𑌂 𑌯𑌮𑌦𑍂𑌤𑌕𑍈𑌃॥௫௧॥  
𑌧𑌾𑌤𑍍𑌰𑍍𑌯𑍈 𑌚𑍈𑌕𑌪𑍍𑌰𑌣𑌾𑌮𑍇𑌨 𑌅𑌶𑍍𑌵𑌮𑍇𑌧𑌾𑌧𑌿𑌕𑌂 𑌫𑌲𑌮𑍍।  
𑌪𑍍𑌰𑌦𑌕𑍍𑌷𑌿𑌣𑌾𑌂 𑌤𑍁 𑌕𑍁𑌰𑍁𑌤𑌾𑌂 𑌸𑌤𑍍𑌯𑌮𑍇𑌤𑌨𑍍𑌮𑌯𑍋𑌦𑌿𑌤𑌮𑍍॥௫௨॥  
𑌬𑍍𑌰𑌾𑌹𑍍𑌮𑌣𑌾𑌨𑍍 𑌸𑌤𑍍𑌯𑌸𑌙𑍍𑌘𑌾𑌂𑌶𑍍𑌚 𑌹𑌰𑌿𑌭𑌕𑍍𑌤𑌿𑌪𑌰𑌾𑌯𑌣𑌾𑌨𑍍।  
𑌭𑍁𑌞𑍍𑌜𑌨𑍍𑌤𑌿 𑌚𑍈𑌵 𑌯𑍇 𑌵𑌿𑌪𑍍𑌰𑌾𑌸𑍍𑌤𑍇𑌷𑌾𑌮𑌨𑍍𑌨𑌂 𑌗𑍁𑌣𑌪𑍍𑌰𑌦𑌮𑍍॥௫௩॥  
𑌧𑌾𑌤𑍍𑌰𑌿𑌚𑍍𑌛𑌾𑌯𑌾𑌂 𑌸𑌮𑌾𑌶𑍍𑌰𑌿𑌤𑍍𑌯 𑌕𑌾𑌰𑍍𑌤𑌿𑌕𑍇𑌽𑌨𑍍𑌨𑌂 𑌤𑍁 𑌭𑍁𑌜𑍍𑌯𑌤𑍇।  
𑌅𑌨𑍍𑌨𑌸𑌂𑌸𑌰𑍍𑌗𑌜𑌂 𑌪𑌾𑌪𑌂 𑌬𑌹𑍁𑌵𑌰𑍍𑌷𑌂 𑌚 𑌨𑌶𑍍𑌯𑌤𑌿॥௫௪॥  
𑌇𑌤𑌿 𑌶𑍍𑌰𑍀𑌪𑌦𑍍𑌮𑌪𑍁𑌰𑌾𑌣𑍇 𑌅𑌕𑍍𑌷𑌯𑌨𑌵𑌮𑍀𑌵𑍍𑌰𑌤𑌕𑌥𑌾 𑌸𑌮𑌾𑌪𑍍𑌤𑌾॥  
  
𑌅𑌥 𑌕𑍂𑌷𑍍𑌮𑌾𑌣𑍍𑌡𑌦𑌾𑌨𑌵𑌿𑌧𑌿𑌃---

847a35eb0c.b: Graha-yuddha (amshu-vimarda) between śaniḥ and śukraḥ in uttaraprōṣṭhapadā mīnaḥ, center-to-center separation 0°54′37.66″.
847a35eb0c.d:
This is an amshu-vimarda (a collision of rays -- the discs themselves do not touch): center-to-center separation 0°54′37.66″, 0°54′24.90″ apart, disc-to-disc. śaniḥ at uttaraprōṣṭhapadā-2 mīnaḥ (latitude 2°07′33.54″ S, Rju (direct), magnitude +0.97, elongation 14°47′55.17″ E). śukraḥ at uttaraprōṣṭhapadā-2 mīnaḥ (latitude 1°12′55.88″ S, Rju (direct), magnitude -3.90, elongation 14°41′52.53″ E). Classical texts weigh both the northern position and the greater apparent brightness/nearness in deciding the victor (jayI) of a yuddha; here śaniḥ is towards the north (traditionally said to prevail), while by brightness/nearness (the larger apparent diameter) śaniḥ is taken as jayI over śukraḥ. A graha-yuddha (also called amshu-vimarda, "collision of rays") occurs when two of the five tArA grahas -- budha, śukra, aṅgāraka, br̥haspati, śanaiśchara -- come within 1 aMsha (60 kalA) of each other in longitude, close enough that they may be difficult to tell apart in the sky. It is called yuddha proper only when their discs actually touch/overlap; otherwise, amshu-vimarda.

The Surya Siddhanta itself cautions that this matter is described only to indicate the auspicious/inauspicious effects for people -- in reality the grahas remain far apart from one another and continue along their own paths. This is not to be received with fear, but as an advance, compassionate intimation from those who calculated these movements accurately, meant to help people take protective measures in time.

Classical texts (e.g. Brihat Samhita ch. 17) weigh both which graha is to the north and which is more prominent (nearer/brighter, of larger apparent diameter) in declaring a victor (jayī) of the yuddha; the defeated (jita) graha's significations are said to suffer for a particular section of society -- this is never a universal ill effect. The traditional response is to increase one's spiritual efforts: japa, homa, dAna and parAyaNa (especially of the Navagraha stotra), with higher AvRtti for the two grahas actually involved, particularly if the day also coincides with some other puNya kAla (e.g. a sAyana saGkramaNa).

Per the Narada Samhita (as cited in Muhurta Chintamani), the nakshatra in which a graha-yuddha occurs should be avoided for auspicious functions (vivAha, upanayana etc.) for six months following the event. If this cannot be avoided, perform parihAra for candra-bala.
847a35eb0c.s:
𑌭𑌾𑌵𑌾𑌭𑌾𑌵𑌾𑌯 𑌲𑍋𑌕𑌾𑌨𑌾𑌂 𑌕𑌲𑍍𑌪𑌨𑍇𑌯𑌂 𑌪𑍍𑌰𑌦𑌰𑍍𑌶𑌿𑌤𑌾।

--𑌸𑍂𑌰𑍍𑌯𑌸𑌿𑌦𑍍𑌧𑌾𑌨𑍍𑌤𑍇

--𑌮𑍁𑌹𑍂𑌰𑍍𑌤𑌚𑌿𑌨𑍍𑌤𑌾𑌮𑌣𑍌 (𑌨𑌾𑌰𑌦𑌸𑌂𑌹𑌿𑌤𑌾𑌨𑍁𑌸𑌾𑌰𑍇𑌣)

847cde4c7f.d:
When Shravana nakshatra falls on a Monday, it is a special yōgaḥ. In the cyclic rotation of time, along with the bad combinations of grahas and nakshatras that indicate the probability of upcoming difficulties, good combinations that grant benefits in multiples also arise. Among such good combinations are the Amrita Siddhi yogas of certain weekdays and nakshatras. They are Sunday-Hasta, Monday-Mrigashirsha, Tuesday-Ashvini, Wednesday-Anuradha, Thursday-Pushya, Friday-Revati, Saturday-Rohini. Good deeds performed on such yogas become especially strong in protecting and nourishing us.
For instance, in Devi Atharvashirsha, it is said bhaumāśvinyāṁ mahādevī-sannidhau japtvā mahāmr̥tyuṁ tarati, that is, one can cross even mahāmr̥tyu by doing parayanam when Tuesday and Ashvini join.
847cde4c7f.s:
𑌆𑌦𑌿𑌤𑍍𑌯𑌹𑌸𑍍𑌤𑍇 𑌗𑍁𑌰𑍁𑌪𑍁𑌷𑍍𑌯𑌯𑍋𑌗𑍇 𑌬𑍁𑌧𑌾𑌨𑍁𑌰𑌾𑌧𑌾 𑌶𑌨𑌿𑌰𑍋𑌹𑌿𑌣𑍀 𑌚।  
𑌸𑍋𑌮𑍇 𑌚 𑌸𑍌𑌮𑍍𑌯𑌂 𑌭𑍃𑌗𑍁𑌰𑍇𑌵𑌤𑍀 𑌚 𑌭𑍌𑌮𑌾𑌶𑍍𑌵𑌿𑌨𑍀 𑌚𑌾𑌮𑍃𑌤𑌸𑌿𑌦𑍍𑌧𑌿𑌯𑍋𑌗𑌾𑌃॥

84a0a112f0.b: Graha-yuddha (amshu-vimarda) between śaniḥ and śukraḥ in rēvatī mīnaḥ, center-to-center separation 0°36′17.02″.
84a0a112f0.d:
This is an amshu-vimarda (a collision of rays -- the discs themselves do not touch): center-to-center separation 0°36′17.02″, 0°36′03.60″ apart, disc-to-disc. śaniḥ at rēvatī-4 mīnaḥ (latitude 2°15′32.09″ S, Rju (direct), magnitude +0.71, elongation 25°42′19.26″ W). śukraḥ at rēvatī-4 mīnaḥ (latitude 1°39′15.08″ S, Rju (direct), magnitude -3.87, elongation 25°39′44.65″ W). Classical texts weigh both the northern position and the greater apparent brightness/nearness in deciding the victor (jayI) of a yuddha; here śaniḥ is towards the north (traditionally said to prevail), while by brightness/nearness (the larger apparent diameter) śaniḥ is taken as jayI over śukraḥ. A graha-yuddha (also called amshu-vimarda, "collision of rays") occurs when two of the five tArA grahas -- budha, śukra, aṅgāraka, br̥haspati, śanaiśchara -- come within 1 aMsha (60 kalA) of each other in longitude, close enough that they may be difficult to tell apart in the sky. It is called yuddha proper only when their discs actually touch/overlap; otherwise, amshu-vimarda.

The Surya Siddhanta itself cautions that this matter is described only to indicate the auspicious/inauspicious effects for people -- in reality the grahas remain far apart from one another and continue along their own paths. This is not to be received with fear, but as an advance, compassionate intimation from those who calculated these movements accurately, meant to help people take protective measures in time.

Classical texts (e.g. Brihat Samhita ch. 17) weigh both which graha is to the north and which is more prominent (nearer/brighter, of larger apparent diameter) in declaring a victor (jayī) of the yuddha; the defeated (jita) graha's significations are said to suffer for a particular section of society -- this is never a universal ill effect. The traditional response is to increase one's spiritual efforts: japa, homa, dAna and parAyaNa (especially of the Navagraha stotra), with higher AvRtti for the two grahas actually involved, particularly if the day also coincides with some other puNya kAla (e.g. a sAyana saGkramaNa).

Per the Narada Samhita (as cited in Muhurta Chintamani), the nakshatra in which a graha-yuddha occurs should be avoided for auspicious functions (vivAha, upanayana etc.) for six months following the event. If this cannot be avoided, perform parihAra for candra-bala.

84a2acc4ca.d: When the transit of the Sun (saṅkrānti) happens in the second half of the day (aparāhṇa) and before midnight, the second half of the day form a puṇyakāla for various observances. In addition to 16 ghatikas on either side of the transition, and specific puṇyakālas like ṣaḍaśīti, viṣṇupadī etc., this is also useful, especially in cases where the other puṇyakālas are inconvenient for appropriate performance of rituals such as snāna, dāna, tarpaṇa, etc.

84a6542930.b: Observed on Paurṇamāsī tithi of Kārttikaḥ (lunar) month (Aparāhṇaḥ/vyaapti).
84a6542930.s:
𑌸𑍍𑌮𑍃𑌤𑍍𑌯𑌨𑍍𑌤𑌰𑍇---  
𑌅𑌮𑌾 𑌪𑌾𑌤𑌶𑍍𑌚 𑌸𑌙𑍍𑌕𑍍𑌰𑌾𑌨𑍍𑌤𑌿𑌸𑍍𑌤𑌥𑌾 𑌵𑍈𑌧𑍃𑌤𑌿𑌰𑍇𑌵 𑌚।  
𑌅𑌷𑍍𑌟𑌕𑌾𑌶𑍍𑌚𑍈𑌵 𑌮𑌨𑍍𑌵𑌾𑌦𑌿𑌰𑍍𑌯𑍁𑌗𑌾𑌦𑌿𑌶𑍍𑌚 𑌮𑌹𑌾𑌲𑌯𑌃॥  
𑌚𑌨𑍍𑌦𑍍𑌰𑌸𑍂𑌰𑍍𑌯𑍋𑌪𑌰𑌾𑌗𑌶𑍍𑌚 𑌗𑌜𑌚𑍍𑌛𑌾𑌯𑌾 𑌤𑌥𑍈𑌵 𑌚।  
𑌦𑍍𑌰𑌵𑍍𑌯𑌬𑍍𑌰𑌾𑌹𑍍𑌮𑌣𑌸𑌮𑍍𑌪𑌤𑍍𑌤𑌿𑌃 𑌶𑍍𑌰𑌾𑌦𑍍𑌧𑌕𑌾𑌲𑌾𑌃 𑌪𑍍𑌰𑌕𑍀𑌰𑍍𑌤𑌿𑌤𑌾𑌃॥  
𑌮𑌨𑍍𑌵𑌨𑍍𑌤𑌰𑌾𑌦𑌯𑍋 𑌮𑌤𑍍𑌸𑍍𑌯𑌪𑍁𑌰𑌾𑌣𑍇 𑌦𑌰𑍍𑌶𑌿𑌤𑌾𑌃---  
𑌆𑌶𑍍𑌵𑌯𑍁𑌕𑍍𑌛𑍁𑌕𑍍𑌲𑌨𑌵𑌮𑍀 𑌕𑌾𑌰𑍍𑌤𑌿𑌕𑍀 𑌦𑍍𑌵𑌾𑌦𑌶𑍀 𑌸𑌿𑌤𑌾।  
𑌤𑍃𑌤𑍀𑌯𑌾 𑌚𑍈𑌤𑍍𑌰𑌮𑌾𑌸𑌸𑍍𑌯 𑌸𑌿𑌤𑌾 𑌭𑌾𑌦𑍍𑌰𑌪𑌦𑌸𑍍𑌯 𑌚॥  
𑌫𑌾𑌲𑍍𑌗𑍁𑌨𑌸𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌪𑍍𑌯𑌮𑌾𑌵𑌾𑌸𑍍𑌯𑌾 𑌪𑍁𑌷𑍍𑌯𑌸𑍍𑌯𑍈𑌕𑌾𑌦𑌶𑍀 𑌸𑌿𑌤𑌾।  
𑌆𑌷𑌾𑌢𑌸𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌪𑌿 𑌦𑌶𑌮𑍀 𑌮𑌾𑌘𑌮𑌾𑌸𑌸𑍍𑌯 𑌸𑌪𑍍𑌤𑌮𑍀॥  
𑌶𑍍𑌰𑌾𑌵𑌣𑌸𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌷𑍍𑌟𑌮𑍀 𑌕𑍃𑌷𑍍𑌣𑌾 𑌤𑌥𑌾𑌽𑌽𑌷𑌾𑌢𑍀 𑌚 𑌪𑍂𑌰𑍍𑌣𑌿𑌮𑌾।  
𑌕𑌾𑌰𑍍𑌤𑌿𑌕𑍀 𑌫𑌾𑌲𑍍𑌗𑍁𑌨𑍀 𑌚𑍈𑌤𑍍𑌰𑍀 𑌜𑍍𑌯𑍈𑌷𑍍𑌠𑍀 𑌪𑌞𑍍𑌚𑌦𑌶𑍀 𑌸𑌿𑌤𑌾॥  
𑌮𑌨𑍍𑌵𑌨𑍍𑌤𑌰𑌾𑌦𑌯𑌶𑍍𑌚𑍈𑌤𑍇 𑌦𑌤𑍍𑌤𑌸𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌕𑍍𑌷𑌯𑌕𑌾𑌰𑌕𑌾𑌃।  
𑌕𑍃𑌤𑌂 𑌶𑍍𑌰𑌾𑌦𑍍𑌧𑌂 𑌵𑌿𑌧𑌾𑌨𑍇𑌨 𑌮𑌨𑍍𑌵𑌾𑌦𑌿𑌷𑍁 𑌯𑍁𑌗𑌾𑌦𑌿𑌷𑍁॥  
𑌹𑌾𑌯𑌨𑌾𑌨𑌿 𑌦𑍍𑌵𑌿𑌸𑌾𑌹𑌸𑍍𑌰𑌂 𑌪𑌿𑌤𑍄𑌣𑌾𑌂 𑌤𑍃𑌪𑍍𑌤𑌿𑌦𑌂 𑌭𑌵𑍇𑌤𑍍।  
𑌆𑌸𑍁 𑌸𑍍𑌨𑌾𑌨𑌂 𑌜𑌪𑍋 𑌹𑍋𑌮𑌃 𑌪𑍁𑌣𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌨𑌨𑍍𑌤𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌯 𑌕𑌲𑍍𑌪𑌤𑍇॥  
𑌮𑌹𑌾𑌭𑌾𑌰𑌤𑍇𑌽𑌪𑌿---   
𑌯𑌾 𑌮𑌨𑍍𑌵𑌾𑌦𑍍𑌯𑌾 𑌯𑍁𑌗𑌾𑌦𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌶𑍍𑌚 𑌤𑌿𑌥𑌯𑌸𑍍𑌤𑌾𑌸𑍁 𑌮𑌾𑌨𑌵𑌃।  
𑌸𑍍𑌨𑌾𑌤𑍍𑌵𑌾 𑌭𑍁𑌕𑍍𑌤𑍍𑌵𑌾 𑌚 𑌦𑌤𑍍𑌤𑍍𑌵𑌾 𑌚 𑌤𑌦𑌨𑌨𑍍𑌤𑌫𑌲𑌂 𑌲𑌭𑍇𑌤𑍍॥  
𑌕𑌾𑌲𑌾𑌦𑌰𑍍𑌶𑍇𑌽𑌪𑌿---  
𑌮𑌨𑍍𑌵𑌾𑌦𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌸𑍁 𑌯𑍁𑌗𑌾𑌦𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌸𑍁 𑌪𑍍𑌰𑌦𑌤𑍍𑌤𑌃 𑌸𑌲𑌿𑌲𑌾𑌞𑍍𑌜𑌲𑌿𑌃।  
𑌸𑌹𑌸𑍍𑌰𑌵𑌾𑌰𑍍𑌷𑌿𑌕𑍀 𑌤𑍃𑌪𑍍𑌤𑌿𑌂 𑌪𑌿𑌤𑍄𑌣𑌾𑌮𑌾𑌵𑌹𑍇𑌤𑍍 𑌪𑌰𑌾𑌮𑍍॥  
𑌦𑍍𑌵𑌿𑌸𑌹𑌸𑍍𑌰𑌾𑌬𑍍𑌦𑌿𑌕𑍀 𑌤𑍃𑌪𑍍𑌤𑌿𑌂 𑌕𑍃𑌤𑌂 𑌶𑍍𑌰𑌾𑌦𑍍𑌧𑌂 𑌯𑌥𑌾𑌵𑌿𑌧𑌿।  
𑌸𑍍𑌨𑌾𑌨𑌂 𑌦𑌾𑌨𑌂 𑌜𑌪𑍋 𑌹𑍋𑌮𑌃 𑌪𑍁𑌣𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌨𑌨𑍍𑌤𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌯 𑌕𑌲𑍍𑌪𑌤𑍇॥  
𑌪𑍁𑌰𑍁𑌷𑌾𑌰𑍍𑌥𑌚𑌿𑌨𑍍𑌤𑌾𑌮𑌣𑍌 𑌮𑌨𑍁𑌃---  
𑌸𑌹𑌸𑍍𑌰𑌗𑍁𑌣𑌿𑌤𑌂 𑌦𑌾𑌨𑌂 𑌭𑌵𑍇𑌦𑍍𑌦𑌤𑍍𑌤𑌂 𑌯𑍁𑌗𑌾𑌦𑌿𑌷𑍁।  
𑌕𑌰𑍍𑌮 𑌶𑍍𑌰𑌾𑌦𑍍𑌧𑌾𑌦𑌿𑌕𑌂 𑌚𑍈𑌵 𑌤𑌥𑌾 𑌮𑌨𑍍𑌵𑌨𑍍𑌤𑌰𑌾𑌦𑌿𑌷𑍁॥

84be232db0.b: Observed on Śukla-Saptamī tithi of Āśvayujaḥ (lunar) month (Aparāhṇaḥ/vyaapti). The event occurred in 4162 (Kali era).
84be232db0.d: Śrīkaṇṭha, son of Śivasāmbapaṇḍita, known by the appellation Parāśiva (Paramaśiva) (after initiation) who remained in the caves of the mountain since initiation governed the Pīṭha for twenty-one years and having placed poet Somaka’s son, Sūrya, in his place, He attained siddhi in the night of saptami of the bright fortnight in the Aśvini month of the year Śārvari. This preceptor Paramaśivendra stayed in the caves of Sahya mountain adhering to the “mode of python” (ajagaravṛtti), restored to by the disciple named Bodhendra, attained siddhi in the Sahya mountain itself.
84be232db0.s:

84ec2acf62.b: Graha-yuddha (amshu-vimarda) between guruḥ and śukraḥ in ārdrā mithunam, center-to-center separation 0°51′41.48″.
84ec2acf62.d:
This is an amshu-vimarda (a collision of rays -- the discs themselves do not touch): center-to-center separation 0°51′41.48″, 0°51′18.53″ apart, disc-to-disc. guruḥ at ārdrā-4 mithunam (latitude 0°03′50.32″ S, Rju (direct), magnitude -1.94, elongation 35°43′04.50″ W). śukraḥ at ārdrā-4 mithunam (latitude 0°55′31.80″ S, Rju (direct), magnitude -3.96, elongation 35°43′41.77″ W). Classical texts weigh both the northern position and the greater apparent brightness/nearness in deciding the victor (jayI) of a yuddha; here śukraḥ is towards the north (traditionally said to prevail), while by brightness/nearness (the larger apparent diameter) guruḥ is taken as jayI over śukraḥ. A graha-yuddha (also called amshu-vimarda, "collision of rays") occurs when two of the five tArA grahas -- budha, śukra, aṅgāraka, br̥haspati, śanaiśchara -- come within 1 aMsha (60 kalA) of each other in longitude, close enough that they may be difficult to tell apart in the sky. It is called yuddha proper only when their discs actually touch/overlap; otherwise, amshu-vimarda.

The Surya Siddhanta itself cautions that this matter is described only to indicate the auspicious/inauspicious effects for people -- in reality the grahas remain far apart from one another and continue along their own paths. This is not to be received with fear, but as an advance, compassionate intimation from those who calculated these movements accurately, meant to help people take protective measures in time.

Classical texts (e.g. Brihat Samhita ch. 17) weigh both which graha is to the north and which is more prominent (nearer/brighter, of larger apparent diameter) in declaring a victor (jayī) of the yuddha; the defeated (jita) graha's significations are said to suffer for a particular section of society -- this is never a universal ill effect. The traditional response is to increase one's spiritual efforts: japa, homa, dAna and parAyaNa (especially of the Navagraha stotra), with higher AvRtti for the two grahas actually involved, particularly if the day also coincides with some other puNya kAla (e.g. a sAyana saGkramaNa).

Per the Narada Samhita (as cited in Muhurta Chintamani), the nakshatra in which a graha-yuddha occurs should be avoided for auspicious functions (vivAha, upanayana etc.) for six months following the event. If this cannot be avoided, perform parihAra for candra-bala.

84fe129f13.d:
The celestial wedding of Bhagavan Srinivasa and Devi Padmavati is a grand festival held annually in the month of Vaishakha. The beautifully adorned Parinayotsavam Mandapam, set amidst the Narayanagiri gardens, serves as the enchanting venue for this three-day event, celebrated under the moonlit sky. The festivities unfold on the auspicious days of Navami, Dashami, and Ekadashi in the month of Vaishakha, featuring Sri Malayappaswami, Shri Venkateshwara's festival deity. Each day, he makes a grand entrance on different Vahanas: the Gaja (elephant), Ashva (horse), and Garuda (eagle), while Devi-s Sridevi and Bhudevi grace the event on separate palanquins.

Following the wedding rituals at the Parinayotsava Mandapam, a traditional 'Koluvu' gathering takes place, filled with the recitation of Vedic hymns and devotional songs. Bhagavan, accompanied by Sridevi and Bhudevi, then majestically returns to the temple.

Each day's festivities are marked by unique traditional rituals. On the first day, the arrival of Bhagavan Malayappa Swami on the celestial Gaja Vahanam, along with his consorts on their palanquins, is a sight to behold. The traditional wedding ceremony is conducted, where Bhagavan is seated in the ornately decorated Parinaya Mandapam, with his consorts positioned opposite him.

The ceremony includes several traditional rituals such as Edurukolu (mutual reception), Pula Bantata (game of flower balls), and Vastra Dharanam (offering of new clothes). These customs are observed over all three days. The grand finale of the divine marriage is marked by a spectacular display of fireworks, adding to the ceremony's splendor. The event concludes with a procession where Bhagavan Malayappa Swami, along with Devi-s Sridevi and Bhudevi, return to the main temple.

855388c052.b: Graha-yuddha (amshu-vimarda) between guruḥ and śukraḥ in ārdrā mithunam, center-to-center separation 0°51′42.41″.
855388c052.d:
This is an amshu-vimarda (a collision of rays -- the discs themselves do not touch): center-to-center separation 0°51′42.41″, 0°51′19.46″ apart, disc-to-disc. guruḥ at ārdrā-4 mithunam (latitude 0°03′50.57″ S, Rju (direct), magnitude -1.94, elongation 35°43′04.67″ W). śukraḥ at ārdrā-4 mithunam (latitude 0°55′32.97″ S, Rju (direct), magnitude -3.96, elongation 35°43′41.93″ W). Classical texts weigh both the northern position and the greater apparent brightness/nearness in deciding the victor (jayI) of a yuddha; here śukraḥ is towards the north (traditionally said to prevail), while by brightness/nearness (the larger apparent diameter) guruḥ is taken as jayI over śukraḥ. A graha-yuddha (also called amshu-vimarda, "collision of rays") occurs when two of the five tArA grahas -- budha, śukra, aṅgāraka, br̥haspati, śanaiśchara -- come within 1 aMsha (60 kalA) of each other in longitude, close enough that they may be difficult to tell apart in the sky. It is called yuddha proper only when their discs actually touch/overlap; otherwise, amshu-vimarda.

The Surya Siddhanta itself cautions that this matter is described only to indicate the auspicious/inauspicious effects for people -- in reality the grahas remain far apart from one another and continue along their own paths. This is not to be received with fear, but as an advance, compassionate intimation from those who calculated these movements accurately, meant to help people take protective measures in time.

Classical texts (e.g. Brihat Samhita ch. 17) weigh both which graha is to the north and which is more prominent (nearer/brighter, of larger apparent diameter) in declaring a victor (jayī) of the yuddha; the defeated (jita) graha's significations are said to suffer for a particular section of society -- this is never a universal ill effect. The traditional response is to increase one's spiritual efforts: japa, homa, dAna and parAyaNa (especially of the Navagraha stotra), with higher AvRtti for the two grahas actually involved, particularly if the day also coincides with some other puNya kAla (e.g. a sAyana saGkramaNa).

Per the Narada Samhita (as cited in Muhurta Chintamani), the nakshatra in which a graha-yuddha occurs should be avoided for auspicious functions (vivAha, upanayana etc.) for six months following the event. If this cannot be avoided, perform parihAra for candra-bala.

85f623791f.s:
𑌸𑍍𑌮𑍃𑌤𑍍𑌯𑌨𑍍𑌤𑌰𑍇---  
𑌅𑌮𑌾 𑌪𑌾𑌤𑌶𑍍𑌚 𑌸𑌙𑍍𑌕𑍍𑌰𑌾𑌨𑍍𑌤𑌿𑌸𑍍𑌤𑌥𑌾 𑌵𑍈𑌧𑍃𑌤𑌿𑌰𑍇𑌵 𑌚।  
𑌅𑌷𑍍𑌟𑌕𑌾𑌶𑍍𑌚𑍈𑌵 𑌮𑌨𑍍𑌵𑌾𑌦𑌿𑌰𑍍𑌯𑍁𑌗𑌾𑌦𑌿𑌶𑍍𑌚 𑌮𑌹𑌾𑌲𑌯𑌃॥  
𑌚𑌨𑍍𑌦𑍍𑌰𑌸𑍂𑌰𑍍𑌯𑍋𑌪𑌰𑌾𑌗𑌶𑍍𑌚 𑌗𑌜𑌚𑍍𑌛𑌾𑌯𑌾 𑌤𑌥𑍈𑌵 𑌚।  
𑌦𑍍𑌰𑌵𑍍𑌯𑌬𑍍𑌰𑌾𑌹𑍍𑌮𑌣𑌸𑌮𑍍𑌪𑌤𑍍𑌤𑌿𑌃 𑌶𑍍𑌰𑌾𑌦𑍍𑌧𑌕𑌾𑌲𑌾𑌃 𑌪𑍍𑌰𑌕𑍀𑌰𑍍𑌤𑌿𑌤𑌾𑌃॥  
𑌅𑌥𑌾𑌷𑍍𑌟𑌕𑌾𑌃। 𑌤𑌾𑌶𑍍𑌚𑌤𑌸𑍍𑌰𑌃 𑌮𑌾𑌰𑍍𑌗𑌶𑍀𑌰𑍍𑌷𑌾𑌦𑌿𑌮𑌾𑌸𑌚𑌤𑍁𑌷𑍍𑌟𑌯𑌾𑌪𑌰𑌪𑌕𑍍𑌷𑌾𑌷𑍍𑌟𑌮𑍍𑌯𑌃 - 𑌤𑌥𑌾 𑌚 𑌶𑍌𑌨𑌕𑌃---  
𑌹𑍇𑌮𑌨𑍍𑌤𑌶𑌿𑌶𑌿𑌰𑌯𑍋𑌶𑍍𑌚𑌤𑍁𑌰𑍍𑌣𑌾𑌮𑌪𑌰𑌪𑌕𑍍𑌷𑌾𑌣𑌾𑌮𑌷𑍍𑌟𑌮𑍀𑌷𑍍𑌵𑌷𑍍𑌟𑌕𑌾𑌃 𑌇𑌤𑌿।  
𑌅𑌤𑍍𑌰 𑌵𑌿𑌶𑍇𑌷𑌮𑌾𑌹 𑌵𑌿𑌷𑍍𑌣𑍁𑌃---  
𑌅𑌷𑍍𑌟𑌕𑌾𑌸𑍍𑌤𑌿𑌸𑍍𑌰𑍋𑌽𑌷𑍍𑌟𑌮𑍍𑌯𑍋𑌽𑌨𑍍𑌵𑌷𑍍𑌟𑌕𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌃 𑌪𑍂𑌰𑍍𑌵𑍇𑌦𑍍𑌯𑍁𑌃 𑌪𑍍𑌰𑍌𑌷𑍍𑌠𑌪𑌦𑍇 𑌹𑍇𑌮𑌨𑍍𑌤𑌶𑌿𑌶𑌿𑌰𑌯𑍋𑌰𑌪𑌰𑌪𑌕𑍍𑌷𑍇𑌷𑍁 𑌇𑌤𑌿। 𑌅𑌨𑍍𑌵𑌷𑍍𑌟𑌕𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌃 - 𑌨𑌵𑌮𑍍𑌯𑌃, 𑌪𑍂𑌰𑍍𑌵𑍇𑌦𑍍𑌯𑍁𑌃 - 𑌸𑌪𑍍𑌤𑌮𑍍𑌯𑌃।  
𑌕𑌾𑌲𑌾𑌦𑌰𑍍𑌶𑍇𑌽𑌪𑌿---  
𑌮𑌾𑌰𑍍𑌗𑌶𑍀𑌰𑍍𑌷𑍇 𑌚 𑌪𑍌𑌷𑍇 𑌚 𑌮𑌾𑌘𑍇 𑌪𑍍𑌰𑍌𑌷𑍍𑌠𑍇 𑌚 𑌫𑌾𑌲𑍍𑌗𑍁𑌨𑍇।  
𑌕𑍃𑌷𑍍𑌣𑌪𑌕𑍍𑌷𑍇𑌷𑍁 𑌪𑍂𑌰𑍍𑌵𑍇𑌦𑍍𑌯𑍁𑌰𑌨𑍍𑌵𑌷𑍍𑌟𑌕𑍍𑌯𑌂 𑌤𑌥𑌾𑌽𑌷𑍍𑌟𑌮𑍀।  
𑌇𑌤𑌿 𑌤𑌿𑌸𑍍𑌰𑍋𑌽𑌷𑍍𑌟𑌕𑌾𑌸𑍍𑌤𑌾𑌸𑍁 𑌶𑍍𑌰𑌾𑌦𑍍𑌧𑌂 𑌕𑍁𑌰𑍍𑌵𑍀𑌤 𑌪𑌾𑌰𑍍𑌵𑌣𑌮𑍍।  
𑌆𑌶𑍍𑌵𑌲𑌾𑌯𑌨𑌃---  
𑌹𑍇𑌮𑌨𑍍𑌤𑌶𑌿𑌶𑌿𑌰𑌰𑍍𑌤𑍍𑌵𑍋𑌸𑍍𑌤𑍁 𑌚𑌤𑍁𑌰𑍍𑌣𑌾𑌮𑌪𑌿 𑌸𑌤𑍍𑌤𑌮𑍈𑌃।  
𑌸𑌮𑌰𑍍𑌥𑍈𑌰𑌷𑍍𑌟𑌕𑌾 𑌕𑌾𑌰𑍍𑌯𑌾 𑌕𑍃𑌷𑍍𑌣𑌾𑌨𑌾𑌮𑌷𑍍𑌟𑌮𑍀𑌷𑍁 𑌚।   
𑌏𑌕𑌸𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌂 𑌹𑌿 𑌤𑍍𑌵𑌶𑌕𑍍𑌤𑍇𑌨 𑌕𑌾𑌰𑍍𑌯𑌾 𑌗𑍃𑌹𑍍𑌯𑌸𑍍𑌯 𑌵𑌰𑍍𑌤𑍍𑌮𑌨𑌾 𑌇𑌤𑌿।  
𑌬𑍋𑌧𑌾𑌯𑌨𑍋𑌽𑌪𑌿---  
𑌉𑌪𑌰𑌿𑌷𑍍𑌟𑌾𑌨𑍍 𑌮𑌾𑌘𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌃 𑌪𑍌𑌰𑍍𑌣𑌮𑌾𑌸𑍍𑌯𑌾 𑌅𑌪𑌰𑌪𑌕𑍍𑌷𑌸𑍍𑌯 𑌸𑌪𑍍𑌤𑌮𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌮𑌷𑍍𑌟𑌮𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌂 𑌨𑌵𑌮𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌮𑌿𑌤𑌿 𑌕𑍍𑌰𑌿𑌯𑍇𑌤𑌾𑌪𑌿 𑌵𑌾𑌽𑌷𑍍𑌟𑌮𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌮𑍇𑌵 𑌇𑌤𑌿।

861a8171a3.b: Graha-yuddha (amshu-vimarda) between guruḥ and budhaḥ in maghā siṁhaḥ, center-to-center separation 0°37′23.97″.
861a8171a3.d:
This is an amshu-vimarda (a collision of rays -- the discs themselves do not touch): center-to-center separation 0°37′23.97″, 0°37′06.42″ apart, disc-to-disc. guruḥ at maghā-4 siṁhaḥ (latitude 0°54′43.29″ N, Rju (direct), magnitude -1.70, elongation 8°32′36.71″ E). budhaḥ at maghā-4 siṁhaḥ (latitude 1°32′07.27″ N, Rju (direct), magnitude -1.11, elongation 8°37′54.16″ E). Classical texts weigh both the northern position and the greater apparent brightness/nearness in deciding the victor (jayI) of a yuddha; here budhaḥ is towards the north (traditionally said to prevail), while by brightness/nearness (the larger apparent diameter) guruḥ is taken as jayI over budhaḥ. A graha-yuddha (also called amshu-vimarda, "collision of rays") occurs when two of the five tArA grahas -- budha, śukra, aṅgāraka, br̥haspati, śanaiśchara -- come within 1 aMsha (60 kalA) of each other in longitude, close enough that they may be difficult to tell apart in the sky. It is called yuddha proper only when their discs actually touch/overlap; otherwise, amshu-vimarda.

The Surya Siddhanta itself cautions that this matter is described only to indicate the auspicious/inauspicious effects for people -- in reality the grahas remain far apart from one another and continue along their own paths. This is not to be received with fear, but as an advance, compassionate intimation from those who calculated these movements accurately, meant to help people take protective measures in time.

Classical texts (e.g. Brihat Samhita ch. 17) weigh both which graha is to the north and which is more prominent (nearer/brighter, of larger apparent diameter) in declaring a victor (jayī) of the yuddha; the defeated (jita) graha's significations are said to suffer for a particular section of society -- this is never a universal ill effect. The traditional response is to increase one's spiritual efforts: japa, homa, dAna and parAyaNa (especially of the Navagraha stotra), with higher AvRtti for the two grahas actually involved, particularly if the day also coincides with some other puNya kAla (e.g. a sAyana saGkramaNa).

Per the Narada Samhita (as cited in Muhurta Chintamani), the nakshatra in which a graha-yuddha occurs should be avoided for auspicious functions (vivAha, upanayana etc.) for six months following the event. If this cannot be avoided, perform parihAra for candra-bala.

863afbe037.b: Partial lunar eclipse (parimāṇa ≈4.5 of 12 aṅgulas), Moon at the Rahu node (puccha/descending).
863afbe037.d: The eclipse is already in progress at moonrise (grastodaya). Umbral magnitude: 0.37 (parimāṇa ≈4.5 of the traditional 12 aṅgulas). Avoid food: 09:27►19:53 (from 3 yaamas before the yaama of first contact, until the eclipse's end). Those with janma nakshatra maghā/pūrvaphalgunī/uttaraphalgunī (preceding/grahaNa/succeeding), or pūrvāṣāḍhā (anujanma) or apabharaṇī (trijanma) get ashubha phala and should consider graha-shanti next day. By rashi: siṁhaḥ, kanyā, makaraḥ, vr̥ṣabhaḥ get more ashubha phala, dhanuḥ, kumbhaḥ, mēṣaḥ, karkaṭaḥ somewhat ashubha, tulā, vr̥śchikaḥ, mīnaḥ, mithunam shubha phala. General notes: Avoid touching anything other than what's needed for the anushthana (especially bed/mat/cloth) until the mokSha snAna after the eclipse ends -- this is grahaNa Ashaucham. Do not sleep or attend to natural impulses during the eclipse. Mantra japa and dAna during the puNya kAla are of immense benefit. Do not view the eclipse with naked eyes. Pregnant women should avoid exposure to the sun/moon's light during the respective eclipse.
863afbe037.r: - Food-restriction timing and graha-shanti nakshatra/rashi lists follow this pancAnga's "General notes for all grahanas" instructions.

𑌅𑌵𑌤𑌾𑌰𑌦𑌿𑌨𑍇 𑌪𑍁𑌣𑍍𑌯𑍇 𑌹𑌰𑌿𑌮𑍁𑌦𑍍𑌦𑌿𑌶𑍍𑌯 𑌭𑌕𑍍𑌤𑌿𑌤𑌃।

—𑌸𑍍𑌮𑍃𑌤𑌿𑌮𑍁𑌕𑍍𑌤𑌾𑌫𑌲𑌮𑍍  
𑌲𑌕𑍍𑌷𑍍𑌮𑍀𑌨𑌾𑌰𑌾𑌯𑌣𑌸𑌂𑌹𑌿𑌤𑌾/𑌖𑌣𑍍𑌡𑌃 ௧ (𑌕𑍃𑌤𑌯𑍁𑌗𑌸𑌨𑍍𑌤𑌾𑌨𑌃)/𑌅𑌧𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌯𑌃 ௨௬௮---  
𑌵𑍈𑌶𑌾𑌖𑌸𑍍𑌯 𑌸𑌿𑌤𑍇 𑌪𑌕𑍍𑌷𑍇 𑌤𑍃𑌤𑍀𑌯𑌾𑌯𑌾𑌂 𑌪𑍁𑌨𑌰𑍍𑌵𑌸𑍌।  
𑌜𑌮𑌦𑌗𑍍𑌨𑌿𑌗𑍃𑌹𑍇 𑌪𑍍𑌰𑌾𑌦𑍁𑌰𑌾𑌸𑍀𑌤𑍍𑌪𑌰𑌶𑍁𑌧𑍃𑌕𑍍 𑌹𑌰𑌿𑌃॥௨௨॥  
𑌵𑍍𑌰𑌤𑌰𑌾𑌜𑍇—  
𑌇𑌯𑌮𑍇𑌵 𑌤𑍃𑌤𑍀𑌯𑌾 𑌪𑌰𑌶𑍁𑌰𑌾𑌮𑌜𑌯𑌨𑍍𑌤𑍀॥ 𑌸𑌾 𑌚 𑌪𑍍𑌰𑌦𑍋𑌷𑌵𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌪𑌿𑌨𑍀 𑌗𑍍𑌰𑌾𑌹𑍍𑌯𑌾।  
𑌤𑌦𑍁𑌕𑍍𑌤𑌂 𑌭𑌾𑌰𑍍𑌗𑌵𑌾𑌰𑍍𑌚𑌨𑌦𑍀𑌪𑌿𑌕𑌾𑌯𑌾𑌂 𑌸𑍍𑌕𑌨𑍍𑌦𑌭𑌵𑌿𑌷𑍍𑌯𑌯𑍋𑌃—  
𑌵𑍈𑌶𑌾𑌖𑌸𑍍𑌯 𑌸𑌿𑌤𑍇 𑌪𑌕𑍍𑌷𑍇 𑌤𑍃𑌤𑍀𑌯𑌾𑌯𑌾𑌂 𑌪𑍁𑌨𑌰𑍍𑌵𑌸𑍌।

869a32be29.b: Event occured on 1737-04-16 (gregorian). Julian date was converted to Gregorian in this reckoning.
869a32be29.d:
On the nightfall, a Maratha contingent attacked Portuguese bastion called St Jeronimo. With the proficient use of gun fire & artillery, finally the Marathas won St Jeronimo bastion. Chimaji Appa named St Jeronimo Bastion as 'Fatteh Buruj' (Bastion of Victory) as it was the first Bastion won by Marathas during this whole campaign.

Impact
This was part of a war that ended the Portuguese "Generalship of the North". The resulting treaty ensured that Gentoos (Hindus) inhabiting Goa etc. could again freely practice their religion. The English (having failed to aid Portuguese) hastily sent envoys to draw up friendship treaties with marATha-s. This victory came at a heavy cost (22k soldiers dead) and after a determined campaign of 2 years.

86a9088e28.b: Graha-yuddha (amshu-vimarda) between budhaḥ and śaniḥ in rēvatī mīnaḥ, center-to-center separation 0°33′52.93″.
86a9088e28.d:
This is an amshu-vimarda (a collision of rays -- the discs themselves do not touch): center-to-center separation 0°33′52.93″, 0°33′42.62″ apart, disc-to-disc. budhaḥ at rēvatī-3 mīnaḥ (latitude 1°40′22.55″ S, Rju (direct), magnitude -1.13, elongation 10°14′15.48″ W). śaniḥ at rēvatī-3 mīnaḥ (latitude 2°14′15.48″ S, Rju (direct), magnitude +0.70, elongation 10°20′37.65″ W). Classical texts weigh both the northern position and the greater apparent brightness/nearness in deciding the victor (jayI) of a yuddha; here śaniḥ is towards the north (traditionally said to prevail), while by brightness/nearness (the larger apparent diameter) śaniḥ is taken as jayI over budhaḥ. A graha-yuddha (also called amshu-vimarda, "collision of rays") occurs when two of the five tArA grahas -- budha, śukra, aṅgāraka, br̥haspati, śanaiśchara -- come within 1 aMsha (60 kalA) of each other in longitude, close enough that they may be difficult to tell apart in the sky. It is called yuddha proper only when their discs actually touch/overlap; otherwise, amshu-vimarda.

The Surya Siddhanta itself cautions that this matter is described only to indicate the auspicious/inauspicious effects for people -- in reality the grahas remain far apart from one another and continue along their own paths. This is not to be received with fear, but as an advance, compassionate intimation from those who calculated these movements accurately, meant to help people take protective measures in time.

Classical texts (e.g. Brihat Samhita ch. 17) weigh both which graha is to the north and which is more prominent (nearer/brighter, of larger apparent diameter) in declaring a victor (jayī) of the yuddha; the defeated (jita) graha's significations are said to suffer for a particular section of society -- this is never a universal ill effect. The traditional response is to increase one's spiritual efforts: japa, homa, dAna and parAyaNa (especially of the Navagraha stotra), with higher AvRtti for the two grahas actually involved, particularly if the day also coincides with some other puNya kAla (e.g. a sAyana saGkramaNa).

Per the Narada Samhita (as cited in Muhurta Chintamani), the nakshatra in which a graha-yuddha occurs should be avoided for auspicious functions (vivAha, upanayana etc.) for six months following the event. If this cannot be avoided, perform parihAra for candra-bala.

872b5fe3f9.b: Graha-yuddha (amshu-vimarda) between aṅgārakaḥ and budhaḥ in rēvatī mīnaḥ, center-to-center separation 0°38′10.47″.
872b5fe3f9.d:
This is an amshu-vimarda (a collision of rays -- the discs themselves do not touch): center-to-center separation 0°38′10.47″, 0°38′06.01″ apart, disc-to-disc. aṅgārakaḥ at rēvatī-2 mīnaḥ (latitude 0°39′31.91″ S, Rju (direct), magnitude +1.10, elongation 3°57′45.46″ W). budhaḥ at rēvatī-2 mīnaḥ (latitude 1°17′42.38″ S, Rju (direct), magnitude -1.68, elongation 4°06′57.40″ W). Classical texts weigh both the northern position and the greater apparent brightness/nearness in deciding the victor (jayI) of a yuddha; here budhaḥ is towards the north (traditionally said to prevail), while by brightness/nearness (the larger apparent diameter) budhaḥ is taken as jayI over aṅgārakaḥ. A graha-yuddha (also called amshu-vimarda, "collision of rays") occurs when two of the five tArA grahas -- budha, śukra, aṅgāraka, br̥haspati, śanaiśchara -- come within 1 aMsha (60 kalA) of each other in longitude, close enough that they may be difficult to tell apart in the sky. It is called yuddha proper only when their discs actually touch/overlap; otherwise, amshu-vimarda.

The Surya Siddhanta itself cautions that this matter is described only to indicate the auspicious/inauspicious effects for people -- in reality the grahas remain far apart from one another and continue along their own paths. This is not to be received with fear, but as an advance, compassionate intimation from those who calculated these movements accurately, meant to help people take protective measures in time.

Classical texts (e.g. Brihat Samhita ch. 17) weigh both which graha is to the north and which is more prominent (nearer/brighter, of larger apparent diameter) in declaring a victor (jayī) of the yuddha; the defeated (jita) graha's significations are said to suffer for a particular section of society -- this is never a universal ill effect. The traditional response is to increase one's spiritual efforts: japa, homa, dAna and parAyaNa (especially of the Navagraha stotra), with higher AvRtti for the two grahas actually involved, particularly if the day also coincides with some other puNya kAla (e.g. a sAyana saGkramaNa).

Per the Narada Samhita (as cited in Muhurta Chintamani), the nakshatra in which a graha-yuddha occurs should be avoided for auspicious functions (vivAha, upanayana etc.) for six months following the event. If this cannot be avoided, perform parihAra for candra-bala.

875d1ee294.d: Even as mogol forces were wasting time trying to capture siMhagaD, shivAjI rapidly advanced to sUrat and surprised everyone. The Governor hid in his castle and sent an emissary who tried to murder shivAjI with his dagger - his hand was cut off by an alert guard, spilling blood on shivAjI. Some marATha-s were upset and cried to kill the prisoners - but shivAjI stopped them in time (as related by English witnesses). After a good sack, the rAjA retreated on 9th. The Dutch Iversen remarked that it was as if shivAjI was fulfilling his dream of pulling Awrangzeb's beard.

This is an amshu-vimarda (a collision of rays -- the discs themselves do not touch): center-to-center separation 0°59′14.92″, 0°59′05.25″ apart, disc-to-disc. budhaḥ at viśākhā-3 tulā (latitude 1°53′49.69″ N, vakra (retrograde), magnitude +2.08, elongation 10°27′48.56″ W). śukraḥ at viśākhā-3 tulā (latitude 0°54′34.78″ N, Rju (direct), magnitude -3.92, elongation 10°19′53.79″ W). Classical texts weigh both the northern position and the greater apparent brightness/nearness in deciding the victor (jayI) of a yuddha; here budhaḥ is towards the north (traditionally said to prevail), while by brightness/nearness (the larger apparent diameter) śukraḥ is taken as jayI over budhaḥ. A graha-yuddha (also called amshu-vimarda, "collision of rays") occurs when two of the five tArA grahas -- budha, śukra, aṅgāraka, br̥haspati, śanaiśchara -- come within 1 aMsha (60 kalA) of each other in longitude, close enough that they may be difficult to tell apart in the sky. It is called yuddha proper only when their discs actually touch/overlap; otherwise, amshu-vimarda.

The Surya Siddhanta itself cautions that this matter is described only to indicate the auspicious/inauspicious effects for people -- in reality the grahas remain far apart from one another and continue along their own paths. This is not to be received with fear, but as an advance, compassionate intimation from those who calculated these movements accurately, meant to help people take protective measures in time.

Classical texts (e.g. Brihat Samhita ch. 17) weigh both which graha is to the north and which is more prominent (nearer/brighter, of larger apparent diameter) in declaring a victor (jayī) of the yuddha; the defeated (jita) graha's significations are said to suffer for a particular section of society -- this is never a universal ill effect. The traditional response is to increase one's spiritual efforts: japa, homa, dAna and parAyaNa (especially of the Navagraha stotra), with higher AvRtti for the two grahas actually involved, particularly if the day also coincides with some other puNya kAla (e.g. a sAyana saGkramaNa).

Per the Narada Samhita (as cited in Muhurta Chintamani), the nakshatra in which a graha-yuddha occurs should be avoided for auspicious functions (vivAha, upanayana etc.) for six months following the event. If this cannot be avoided, perform parihAra for candra-bala.

876d1091f6.b: Observed on Rōhiṇī nakshatra of Mēṣaḥ (sidereal solar) month (Prātaḥ/paraviddha).
876d1091f6.d:
Between the 6th and 9th centuries, in South India, there existed 63 ardent devotees of Bhagavan Shiva, collectively known as the Nayanmars. These devout individuals, hailing from various walks of life including potters, fishermen, farmers, merchants, priests, hunters, and washermen, created devotional songs still sung by followers around the globe. Among these Nayanmars, Appar, Sambandar, and Sundarar, known for their Thevaram hymns, along with Manikkavasagar, are distinguished as the Samayacharyas or the ‘The Four’ (nālvar) revered teachers of the faith. They were instrumental in promoting the Shaiva Siddhanta philosophy and culture, effectively challenging the spread of Jainism and Buddhism. Their teachings centered around the concept that Shiva embodies love, and that embracing love for all beings and existence is essential in connecting with Shiva, the Supreme Being.

Mangaiyarkarasiyar, the 50th of the Nayanmars was the wife of another Nayanmar, Ninra Seer Nadumara Nayanmar, who was earlier known as Koon Pandyan, the hunchbacked Pandyan king of Madurai. Tiru Jnana Sambandar, a revered Nayanmar, arrived in Madurai and was invited into the city by Kulacchirai Nayanmar. Despite attempts by the Jains to harm Sambandar, his divine singing miraculously cured the king of his hunchback and alleviated his pain, leading to his return to Shaivism. Following his conversion, the king conquered northern kings at Tirunelveli, spreading Shaivism in those regions with the support of his wife. Both he and Mangayarkarasiyar deeply revered Sambandar and their dedication to their guru and Shaivism ultimately brought them divine grace.
876d1091f6.r: - 63 Nayanmar Saints by Swami Sivananda, published by The Divine Life Society

876f0fd942.d:
The Phalguna Paurnami festival is a grand five-day celebration held annually at the Swami Pushkarini. Each day of the festival features a different set of deities taken for a celestial ride on a beautifully decorated float in the temple tank.

1. On the first day, Bhagavan Rama, along with Sita and Lakshmana, are worshipped and taken for a ride on the float.
2. The second day is dedicated to Bhagavan Krishna and Rukmini, who are also offered puja and taken on the float for a pleasure ride.

For the last three days, from Trayodashi to Paurnami:
1. Sri Malayappa Swami, accompanied by Sridevi and Bhudevi, are taken out for a ride in the temple tank.
2. The third day includes three rounds of the float, increasing to five rounds on the next day.
3. On the final day, the utsava murtis (festival deities) are taken for a splendid ride on the float for seven rounds, attracting a large number of pilgrims. The beauty of the deities is further enhanced by the charm of the full moon, making this day particularly special and visually stunning.

Those with janma nakshatra śatabhiṣak/pūrvaprōṣṭhapadā/uttaraprōṣṭhapadā (preceding/grahaNa/succeeding), or punarvasuḥ (anujanma) or viśākhā (trijanma) get ashubha phala and should consider graha-shanti next day. General notes: Avoid touching anything other than what's needed for the anushthana (especially bed/mat/cloth) until the mokSha snAna after the eclipse ends -- this is grahaNa Ashaucham. Do not sleep or attend to natural impulses during the eclipse. Mantra japa and dAna during the puNya kAla are of immense benefit. Do not view the eclipse with naked eyes. Pregnant women should avoid exposure to the sun/moon's light during the respective eclipse.

890d73ddad.b: Graha-yuddha (amshu-vimarda) between aṅgārakaḥ and śukraḥ in pūrvāṣāḍhā dhanuḥ, center-to-center separation 0°10′25.86″.
890d73ddad.d:
This is an amshu-vimarda (a collision of rays -- the discs themselves do not touch): center-to-center separation 0°10′25.86″, 0°10′19.04″ apart, disc-to-disc. aṅgārakaḥ at pūrvāṣāḍhā-4 dhanuḥ (latitude 0°56′02.87″ S, Rju (direct), magnitude +1.08, elongation 0°59′33.28″ E). śukraḥ at pūrvāṣāḍhā-4 dhanuḥ (latitude 0°45′37.01″ S, Rju (direct), magnitude -3.91, elongation 0°49′52.70″ E). Classical texts weigh both the northern position and the greater apparent brightness/nearness in deciding the victor (jayI) of a yuddha; here aṅgārakaḥ is towards the north (traditionally said to prevail), while by brightness/nearness (the larger apparent diameter) śukraḥ is taken as jayI over aṅgārakaḥ. A graha-yuddha (also called amshu-vimarda, "collision of rays") occurs when two of the five tArA grahas -- budha, śukra, aṅgāraka, br̥haspati, śanaiśchara -- come within 1 aMsha (60 kalA) of each other in longitude, close enough that they may be difficult to tell apart in the sky. It is called yuddha proper only when their discs actually touch/overlap; otherwise, amshu-vimarda.

The Surya Siddhanta itself cautions that this matter is described only to indicate the auspicious/inauspicious effects for people -- in reality the grahas remain far apart from one another and continue along their own paths. This is not to be received with fear, but as an advance, compassionate intimation from those who calculated these movements accurately, meant to help people take protective measures in time.

Classical texts (e.g. Brihat Samhita ch. 17) weigh both which graha is to the north and which is more prominent (nearer/brighter, of larger apparent diameter) in declaring a victor (jayī) of the yuddha; the defeated (jita) graha's significations are said to suffer for a particular section of society -- this is never a universal ill effect. The traditional response is to increase one's spiritual efforts: japa, homa, dAna and parAyaNa (especially of the Navagraha stotra), with higher AvRtti for the two grahas actually involved, particularly if the day also coincides with some other puNya kAla (e.g. a sAyana saGkramaNa).

Per the Narada Samhita (as cited in Muhurta Chintamani), the nakshatra in which a graha-yuddha occurs should be avoided for auspicious functions (vivAha, upanayana etc.) for six months following the event. If this cannot be avoided, perform parihAra for candra-bala.

At this moment śukraḥ is at anūrādhā-1 vr̥śchikaḥ (latitude 0°44′12.73″ N, moving r̥ju (direct)), magnitude -3.92, elongation 9°05′39.89″ W of the Sun. 897036de74.b: Graha-yuddha (amshu-vimarda) between budhaḥ and śaniḥ in rēvatī mīnaḥ, center-to-center separation 0°33′54.38″.
897036de74.d:
This is an amshu-vimarda (a collision of rays -- the discs themselves do not touch): center-to-center separation 0°33′54.38″, 0°33′44.06″ apart, disc-to-disc. budhaḥ at rēvatī-3 mīnaḥ (latitude 1°40′20.90″ S, Rju (direct), magnitude -1.13, elongation 10°14′15.58″ W). śaniḥ at rēvatī-3 mīnaḥ (latitude 2°14′15.27″ S, Rju (direct), magnitude +0.70, elongation 10°20′38.09″ W). Classical texts weigh both the northern position and the greater apparent brightness/nearness in deciding the victor (jayI) of a yuddha; here śaniḥ is towards the north (traditionally said to prevail), while by brightness/nearness (the larger apparent diameter) śaniḥ is taken as jayI over budhaḥ. A graha-yuddha (also called amshu-vimarda, "collision of rays") occurs when two of the five tArA grahas -- budha, śukra, aṅgāraka, br̥haspati, śanaiśchara -- come within 1 aMsha (60 kalA) of each other in longitude, close enough that they may be difficult to tell apart in the sky. It is called yuddha proper only when their discs actually touch/overlap; otherwise, amshu-vimarda.

The Surya Siddhanta itself cautions that this matter is described only to indicate the auspicious/inauspicious effects for people -- in reality the grahas remain far apart from one another and continue along their own paths. This is not to be received with fear, but as an advance, compassionate intimation from those who calculated these movements accurately, meant to help people take protective measures in time.

Classical texts (e.g. Brihat Samhita ch. 17) weigh both which graha is to the north and which is more prominent (nearer/brighter, of larger apparent diameter) in declaring a victor (jayī) of the yuddha; the defeated (jita) graha's significations are said to suffer for a particular section of society -- this is never a universal ill effect. The traditional response is to increase one's spiritual efforts: japa, homa, dAna and parAyaNa (especially of the Navagraha stotra), with higher AvRtti for the two grahas actually involved, particularly if the day also coincides with some other puNya kAla (e.g. a sAyana saGkramaNa).

Per the Narada Samhita (as cited in Muhurta Chintamani), the nakshatra in which a graha-yuddha occurs should be avoided for auspicious functions (vivAha, upanayana etc.) for six months following the event. If this cannot be avoided, perform parihAra for candra-bala.

897c46f311.b: Observed on Śukla-Prathamā tithi of Kārttikaḥ (lunar) month (Madhyāhnaḥ/paraviddha).
897c46f311.d: Observed on the day after dīpāvalī, on the , Govardhana Puja or annakūṭotsava involves constructing and worshipping a symbolic mountain of food to honour the Govardhana Hill and Bhagavan Krishna. The rituals include preparing a vast array of cooked dishes and dairy products, with the goal of achieving all worldly and spiritual success. On this day, cows are decorated, and worshipped as a form of Lakshmi Devi, with devotees praying for the removal of sins and the attainment of mōksha.
897c46f311.s:
𑌗𑍋𑌵𑌰𑍍𑌧𑌨 𑌧𑌰𑌾𑌧𑌾𑌰 𑌗𑍋𑌕𑍁𑌲𑌤𑍍𑌰𑌾𑌣𑌕𑌾𑌰𑌕।  
𑌵𑌿𑌷𑍍𑌣𑍁𑌬𑌾𑌹𑍁𑌕𑍃𑌤𑍋𑌚𑍍𑌛𑍍𑌰𑌾𑌯 𑌗𑌵𑌾𑌂 𑌕𑍋𑌟𑌿𑌪𑍍𑌰𑌦𑍋 𑌭𑌵॥  
𑌨𑌾𑌰𑌦𑍀𑌯𑌪𑍁𑌰𑌾𑌣𑍇 ௧௧௦ 𑌅𑌧𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌯𑍇---  
𑌅𑌥𑍋𑌰𑍍𑌜𑌸𑌿𑌤𑌪𑌕𑍍𑌷𑌤𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌂 𑌨𑌵𑌰𑌾𑌤𑍍𑌰𑍋𑌦𑌿𑌤𑌂 𑌚𑌰𑍇𑌤𑍍।  
𑌵𑌿𑌶𑍇𑌷𑌾𑌦𑌨𑍍𑌨𑌕𑍂𑌟𑌾𑌖𑍍𑌯𑌂 𑌵𑌿𑌷𑍍𑌣𑍁𑌪𑍍𑌰𑍀𑌤𑌿𑌵𑌿𑌵𑌰𑍍𑌧𑌨𑌮𑍍॥௩௫॥  
𑌸𑌰𑍍𑌵𑌪𑌾𑌕𑍈𑌃 𑌸𑌰𑍍𑌦𑌦𑍋𑌹𑍈𑌃 𑌸𑌰𑍍𑌵𑍈𑌃 𑌸𑌰𑍍𑌵𑌾𑌰𑍍𑌥𑌸𑌿𑌦𑍍𑌧𑌯𑍇॥  
𑌕𑌰𑍍𑌤𑌵𑍍𑌯𑌮𑌨𑍍𑌨𑌕𑍂𑌟𑌂 𑌤𑍁 𑌗𑍋𑌵𑌰𑍍𑌦𑍍𑌧𑌨𑌸𑌮𑌰𑍍𑌚𑌨𑍇॥௩௬॥  
𑌸𑌾𑌯𑌂 𑌗𑍋𑌭𑌿𑌃 𑌸𑌹 𑌶𑍍𑌰𑍀𑌮𑌦𑍍𑌗𑍋𑌵𑌰𑍍𑌦𑍍𑌧𑌨𑌧𑌰𑌾𑌧𑌰𑌮𑍍॥  
𑌸𑌮𑌰𑍍𑌚𑍍𑌯 𑌦𑌕𑍍𑌷𑌿𑌣𑍀𑌕𑍃𑌤𑍍𑌯 𑌭𑍁𑌕𑍍𑌤𑌿𑌮𑍁𑌕𑍍𑌤𑍀 𑌸𑌮𑌾𑌪𑍍𑌨𑍁𑌯𑌾𑌤𑍍॥௩௭॥  
𑌸𑍍𑌕𑌾𑌨𑍍𑌦𑍇 𑌮𑌹𑌾𑌪𑍁𑌰𑌾𑌣 𑌏𑌕𑌾𑌶𑍀𑌤𑌿𑌸𑌾𑌹𑌸𑍍𑌰𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌂 𑌸𑌂𑌹𑌿𑌤𑌾𑌯𑌾𑌂 𑌦𑍍𑌵𑌿𑌤𑍀𑌯𑍇 𑌵𑍈𑌷𑍍𑌣𑌵𑌖𑌣𑍍𑌡𑍇 𑌕𑌾𑌰𑍍𑌤𑌿𑌕𑌮𑌾𑌸𑌮𑌾𑌹𑌾𑌤𑍍𑌮𑍍𑌯𑍇 𑌕𑌾𑌰𑍍𑌤𑌿𑌕𑌶𑍁𑌕𑍍𑌲𑌪𑍍𑌰𑌤𑌿𑌪𑌨𑍍𑌮𑌾𑌹𑌾𑌤𑍍𑌮𑍍𑌯𑌵𑌰𑍍𑌣𑌨𑌂 𑌨𑌾𑌮 𑌦𑌶𑌮𑍋𑌽𑌧𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌯𑍇---  
𑌪𑍍𑌰𑌾𑌤𑌰𑍍𑌗𑍋𑌵𑌰𑍍𑌧𑌨𑌃 𑌪𑍂𑌜𑍍𑌯𑍋 𑌦𑍍𑌯𑍂𑌤𑌂 𑌰𑌾𑌤𑍍𑌰𑍌 𑌸𑌮𑌾𑌚𑌰𑍇𑌤𑍍॥௨௨॥  
𑌭𑍂𑌷𑌣𑍀𑌯𑌾𑌸𑍍𑌤𑌦𑌾 𑌗𑌾𑌵𑍋 𑌵𑌰𑍍𑌜𑍍𑌯𑌾 𑌵𑌹𑌨𑌦𑍋𑌹𑌨𑌾𑌤𑍍॥௨௩॥  
𑌗𑍋𑌵𑌰𑍍𑌧𑌨 𑌧𑌰𑌾𑌧𑌾𑌰 𑌗𑍋𑌕𑍁𑌲𑌤𑍍𑌰𑌾𑌣𑌕𑌾𑌰𑌕।  
𑌵𑌿𑌷𑍍𑌣𑍁𑌬𑌾𑌹𑍁𑌕𑍃𑌤𑍋𑌚𑍍𑌛𑍍𑌰𑌾𑌯 𑌗𑌵𑌾𑌂 𑌕𑍋𑌟𑌿𑌪𑍍𑌰𑌦𑍋 𑌭𑌵॥௨௪॥  
𑌯𑌾 𑌲𑌕𑍍𑌷𑍍𑌮𑍀𑌰𑍍𑌲𑍋𑌕𑌪𑌾𑌲𑌾𑌨𑌾𑌂 𑌧𑍇𑌨𑍁𑌰𑍂𑌪𑍇𑌣 𑌸𑌂𑌸𑍍𑌥𑌿𑌤𑌾।  
𑌘𑍃𑌤𑌂 𑌵𑌹𑌤𑌿 𑌯𑌜𑍍𑌞𑌾𑌰𑍍𑌥𑍇 𑌮𑌮 𑌪𑌾𑌪𑌂 𑌵𑍍𑌯𑌪𑍋𑌹𑌤𑍁॥௨௫॥  
𑌅𑌗𑍍𑌰𑌤𑌃 𑌸𑌨𑍍𑌤𑍁 𑌮𑍇 𑌗𑌾𑌵𑍋 𑌗𑌾𑌵𑍋 𑌮𑍇 𑌸𑌨𑍍𑌤𑍁 𑌪𑍃𑌷𑍍𑌠𑌤𑌃।  
𑌗𑌾𑌵𑍋 𑌮𑍇 𑌹𑍃𑌦𑌯𑌂 𑌸𑌨𑍍𑌤𑍁 𑌗𑌵𑌾𑌂 𑌮𑌧𑍍𑌯𑍇 𑌵𑌸𑌾𑌮𑍍𑌯𑌹𑌮𑍍॥௨௬॥

89812e731e.d: The Brahmotsavam of Nataraja at Chidambaram happens specially around the Aani Thirumanjana festival each year, for ten days. On this day, Nataraja gives darshan on a bhūta vahanam.

898ea54498.b: Event occured on 1665-02-15 (gregorian). Julian date was converted to Gregorian in this reckoning.
898ea54498.d: (Date from shivapur chronology). shivAjI set out from mAlvan with a fleet of 85 frigates and 3 great ships. He plundered barsUr of the ikkeri kingdom (which was in a phase of degeneracy and susceptibility to the Portuguese after the passing of great shivappa). Then he turned to gokArNa-tIrtha for a sacred bath. Then he resumed on the plundering expedition to kArvAr.

89911d0894.b: Observed on Mr̥gaśīrṣam nakshatra of Dhanuḥ (sidereal solar) month (Sūryōdayaḥ/puurvaviddha).

89982b0406.b: Partial lunar eclipse (parimāṇa ≈4.6 of 12 aṅgulas), Moon at the Rahu node (puccha/descending).
89982b0406.d: The eclipse is already in progress at moonrise (grastodaya). Umbral magnitude: 0.38 (parimāṇa ≈4.6 of the traditional 12 aṅgulas). Avoid food: 09:26►19:53 (from 3 yaamas before the yaama of first contact, until the eclipse's end). Those with janma nakshatra maghā/pūrvaphalgunī/uttaraphalgunī (preceding/grahaNa/succeeding), or pūrvāṣāḍhā (anujanma) or apabharaṇī (trijanma) get ashubha phala and should consider graha-shanti next day. By rashi: siṁhaḥ, kanyā, makaraḥ, vr̥ṣabhaḥ get more ashubha phala, dhanuḥ, kumbhaḥ, mēṣaḥ, karkaṭaḥ somewhat ashubha, tulā, vr̥śchikaḥ, mīnaḥ, mithunam shubha phala. General notes: Avoid touching anything other than what's needed for the anushthana (especially bed/mat/cloth) until the mokSha snAna after the eclipse ends -- this is grahaNa Ashaucham. Do not sleep or attend to natural impulses during the eclipse. Mantra japa and dAna during the puNya kAla are of immense benefit. Do not view the eclipse with naked eyes. Pregnant women should avoid exposure to the sun/moon's light during the respective eclipse.
89982b0406.r: - Food-restriction timing and graha-shanti nakshatra/rashi lists follow this pancAnga's "General notes for all grahanas" instructions.

89b35a0165.d: Śaniḥ rises out of combustion (udayaH), heading prāk (east), on 2026-Apr-19 19:29. At this moment śaniḥ is at uttaraprōṣṭhapadā-4 mīnaḥ (latitude 2°09′00.01″ S, moving r̥ju (direct)), magnitude +0.93, elongation 21°48′14.25″ W of the Sun. Emergence from combustion restores a graha's full strength; this is generally considered an auspicious time to begin activities connected with śaniḥ's significations.

89b7358cbf.d: Guruḥ enters vArdhakya (old age) on 2025-May-26 18:55, 15 days before it sets into combustion (mAudhyam). At this moment guruḥ is at mr̥gaśīrṣam-3 mithunam (latitude 0°11′18.77″ S, moving r̥ju (direct)), magnitude -1.92, elongation 21°14′57.97″ E of the Sun. A graha in vArdhakya is considered weakened, giving reduced results, though less so than in outright mAudhya.

89da619e61.d:
Farid-ud-din Shaikh and Ashfak Shaikh came dressed in saffron kurtas to give Kamalesh Tiwari a sweets box (hiding a knife and pistol there), slit his throat and shot him. According to the police, the pistol and sweets used in the murder were bought in Surat and the murder was planned in Dubai. Several conspirators were arrested.

Context: In Dec 2015, Arun Jaitley supported decriminalization of homosexuality. Azam Khan (a criminal politician who would be jailed and illegal property seized a few years later) called RSS members homosexuals. Tiwari retaliated saying that Muhammad was the first homosexual. Tiwari was arrested and jailed for a few months, even as lakhs of muslims went into frenzy.

8a80989174.d: It is said in Vishnu Purāṇam that when Amavasya overlaps with one of nine nakshatras---Anuradha, Vishakha, Swati, Pushya, Ardra, Punarvasu, Shravishtha, Purvaproshthapada, or Shatabhishak---it is sacred even for Devas. For instance, Shraaddha done on an Amavasya joined with Anuradha, Vishakha, Swati keeps the pitrs satisfied for eight years. Likewise, on Pushya, Ardra and Punarvasu, the pitrs are satisfied for twelve years. It is said in the Smrtis, that if Amavasya falls on a Monday, Tuesday or Thursday, such a tithi is given the appellation puṣkalā and is as sacred as a solar eclipse. amāvāsyā of māgha month.

8ab2eeab11.b: Graha-yuddha (amshu-vimarda) between guruḥ and budhaḥ in maghā siṁhaḥ, center-to-center separation 0°37′24.18″.
8ab2eeab11.d:
This is an amshu-vimarda (a collision of rays -- the discs themselves do not touch): center-to-center separation 0°37′24.18″, 0°37′06.62″ apart, disc-to-disc. guruḥ at maghā-4 siṁhaḥ (latitude 0°54′43.34″ N, Rju (direct), magnitude -1.70, elongation 8°32′36.98″ E). budhaḥ at maghā-4 siṁhaḥ (latitude 1°32′07.52″ N, Rju (direct), magnitude -1.11, elongation 8°37′54.43″ E). Classical texts weigh both the northern position and the greater apparent brightness/nearness in deciding the victor (jayI) of a yuddha; here budhaḥ is towards the north (traditionally said to prevail), while by brightness/nearness (the larger apparent diameter) guruḥ is taken as jayI over budhaḥ. A graha-yuddha (also called amshu-vimarda, "collision of rays") occurs when two of the five tArA grahas -- budha, śukra, aṅgāraka, br̥haspati, śanaiśchara -- come within 1 aMsha (60 kalA) of each other in longitude, close enough that they may be difficult to tell apart in the sky. It is called yuddha proper only when their discs actually touch/overlap; otherwise, amshu-vimarda.

The Surya Siddhanta itself cautions that this matter is described only to indicate the auspicious/inauspicious effects for people -- in reality the grahas remain far apart from one another and continue along their own paths. This is not to be received with fear, but as an advance, compassionate intimation from those who calculated these movements accurately, meant to help people take protective measures in time.

Classical texts (e.g. Brihat Samhita ch. 17) weigh both which graha is to the north and which is more prominent (nearer/brighter, of larger apparent diameter) in declaring a victor (jayī) of the yuddha; the defeated (jita) graha's significations are said to suffer for a particular section of society -- this is never a universal ill effect. The traditional response is to increase one's spiritual efforts: japa, homa, dAna and parAyaNa (especially of the Navagraha stotra), with higher AvRtti for the two grahas actually involved, particularly if the day also coincides with some other puNya kAla (e.g. a sAyana saGkramaNa).

Per the Narada Samhita (as cited in Muhurta Chintamani), the nakshatra in which a graha-yuddha occurs should be avoided for auspicious functions (vivAha, upanayana etc.) for six months following the event. If this cannot be avoided, perform parihAra for candra-bala.

𑌸𑍍𑌮𑍃𑌤𑍍𑌯𑌨𑍍𑌤𑌰𑍇---  
𑌅𑌮𑌾 𑌪𑌾𑌤𑌶𑍍𑌚 𑌸𑌙𑍍𑌕𑍍𑌰𑌾𑌨𑍍𑌤𑌿𑌸𑍍𑌤𑌥𑌾 𑌵𑍈𑌧𑍃𑌤𑌿𑌰𑍇𑌵 𑌚।  
𑌅𑌷𑍍𑌟𑌕𑌾𑌶𑍍𑌚𑍈𑌵 𑌮𑌨𑍍𑌵𑌾𑌦𑌿𑌰𑍍𑌯𑍁𑌗𑌾𑌦𑌿𑌶𑍍𑌚 𑌮𑌹𑌾𑌲𑌯𑌃॥  
𑌚𑌨𑍍𑌦𑍍𑌰𑌸𑍂𑌰𑍍𑌯𑍋𑌪𑌰𑌾𑌗𑌶𑍍𑌚 𑌗𑌜𑌚𑍍𑌛𑌾𑌯𑌾 𑌤𑌥𑍈𑌵 𑌚।  
𑌦𑍍𑌰𑌵𑍍𑌯𑌬𑍍𑌰𑌾𑌹𑍍𑌮𑌣𑌸𑌮𑍍𑌪𑌤𑍍𑌤𑌿𑌃 𑌶𑍍𑌰𑌾𑌦𑍍𑌧𑌕𑌾𑌲𑌾𑌃 𑌪𑍍𑌰𑌕𑍀𑌰𑍍𑌤𑌿𑌤𑌾𑌃॥  
𑌅𑌥𑌾𑌷𑍍𑌟𑌕𑌾𑌃। 𑌤𑌾𑌶𑍍𑌚𑌤𑌸𑍍𑌰𑌃 𑌮𑌾𑌰𑍍𑌗𑌶𑍀𑌰𑍍𑌷𑌾𑌦𑌿𑌮𑌾𑌸𑌚𑌤𑍁𑌷𑍍𑌟𑌯𑌾𑌪𑌰𑌪𑌕𑍍𑌷𑌾𑌷𑍍𑌟𑌮𑍍𑌯𑌃 - 𑌤𑌥𑌾 𑌚 𑌶𑍌𑌨𑌕𑌃---  
𑌹𑍇𑌮𑌨𑍍𑌤𑌶𑌿𑌶𑌿𑌰𑌯𑍋𑌶𑍍𑌚𑌤𑍁𑌰𑍍𑌣𑌾𑌮𑌪𑌰𑌪𑌕𑍍𑌷𑌾𑌣𑌾𑌮𑌷𑍍𑌟𑌮𑍀𑌷𑍍𑌵𑌷𑍍𑌟𑌕𑌾𑌃 𑌇𑌤𑌿।  
𑌅𑌤𑍍𑌰 𑌵𑌿𑌶𑍇𑌷𑌮𑌾𑌹 𑌵𑌿𑌷𑍍𑌣𑍁𑌃---  
𑌅𑌷𑍍𑌟𑌕𑌾𑌸𑍍𑌤𑌿𑌸𑍍𑌰𑍋𑌽𑌷𑍍𑌟𑌮𑍍𑌯𑍋𑌽𑌨𑍍𑌵𑌷𑍍𑌟𑌕𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌃 𑌪𑍂𑌰𑍍𑌵𑍇𑌦𑍍𑌯𑍁𑌃 𑌪𑍍𑌰𑍌𑌷𑍍𑌠𑌪𑌦𑍇 𑌹𑍇𑌮𑌨𑍍𑌤𑌶𑌿𑌶𑌿𑌰𑌯𑍋𑌰𑌪𑌰𑌪𑌕𑍍𑌷𑍇𑌷𑍁 𑌇𑌤𑌿। 𑌅𑌨𑍍𑌵𑌷𑍍𑌟𑌕𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌃 - 𑌨𑌵𑌮𑍍𑌯𑌃, 𑌪𑍂𑌰𑍍𑌵𑍇𑌦𑍍𑌯𑍁𑌃 - 𑌸𑌪𑍍𑌤𑌮𑍍𑌯𑌃।  
𑌕𑌾𑌲𑌾𑌦𑌰𑍍𑌶𑍇𑌽𑌪𑌿---  
𑌮𑌾𑌰𑍍𑌗𑌶𑍀𑌰𑍍𑌷𑍇 𑌚 𑌪𑍌𑌷𑍇 𑌚 𑌮𑌾𑌘𑍇 𑌪𑍍𑌰𑍌𑌷𑍍𑌠𑍇 𑌚 𑌫𑌾𑌲𑍍𑌗𑍁𑌨𑍇।  
𑌕𑍃𑌷𑍍𑌣𑌪𑌕𑍍𑌷𑍇𑌷𑍁 𑌪𑍂𑌰𑍍𑌵𑍇𑌦𑍍𑌯𑍁𑌰𑌨𑍍𑌵𑌷𑍍𑌟𑌕𑍍𑌯𑌂 𑌤𑌥𑌾𑌽𑌷𑍍𑌟𑌮𑍀।  
𑌇𑌤𑌿 𑌤𑌿𑌸𑍍𑌰𑍋𑌽𑌷𑍍𑌟𑌕𑌾𑌸𑍍𑌤𑌾𑌸𑍁 𑌶𑍍𑌰𑌾𑌦𑍍𑌧𑌂 𑌕𑍁𑌰𑍍𑌵𑍀𑌤 𑌪𑌾𑌰𑍍𑌵𑌣𑌮𑍍।  
𑌆𑌶𑍍𑌵𑌲𑌾𑌯𑌨𑌃---  
𑌹𑍇𑌮𑌨𑍍𑌤𑌶𑌿𑌶𑌿𑌰𑌰𑍍𑌤𑍍𑌵𑍋𑌸𑍍𑌤𑍁 𑌚𑌤𑍁𑌰𑍍𑌣𑌾𑌮𑌪𑌿 𑌸𑌤𑍍𑌤𑌮𑍈𑌃।  
𑌸𑌮𑌰𑍍𑌥𑍈𑌰𑌷𑍍𑌟𑌕𑌾 𑌕𑌾𑌰𑍍𑌯𑌾 𑌕𑍃𑌷𑍍𑌣𑌾𑌨𑌾𑌮𑌷𑍍𑌟𑌮𑍀𑌷𑍁 𑌚।   
𑌏𑌕𑌸𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌂 𑌹𑌿 𑌤𑍍𑌵𑌶𑌕𑍍𑌤𑍇𑌨 𑌕𑌾𑌰𑍍𑌯𑌾 𑌗𑍃𑌹𑍍𑌯𑌸𑍍𑌯 𑌵𑌰𑍍𑌤𑍍𑌮𑌨𑌾 𑌇𑌤𑌿।  
𑌬𑍋𑌧𑌾𑌯𑌨𑍋𑌽𑌪𑌿---  
𑌉𑌪𑌰𑌿𑌷𑍍𑌟𑌾𑌨𑍍 𑌮𑌾𑌘𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌃 𑌪𑍌𑌰𑍍𑌣𑌮𑌾𑌸𑍍𑌯𑌾 𑌅𑌪𑌰𑌪𑌕𑍍𑌷𑌸𑍍𑌯 𑌸𑌪𑍍𑌤𑌮𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌮𑌷𑍍𑌟𑌮𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌂 𑌨𑌵𑌮𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌮𑌿𑌤𑌿 𑌕𑍍𑌰𑌿𑌯𑍇𑌤𑌾𑌪𑌿 𑌵𑌾𑌽𑌷𑍍𑌟𑌮𑍍𑌯𑌾𑌮𑍇𑌵 𑌇𑌤𑌿।

8b492b5301.b: Graha-yuddha (amshu-vimarda) between aṅgārakaḥ and budhaḥ in uttarāṣāḍhā makaraḥ, center-to-center separation 0°41′01.51″.
8b492b5301.d:
This is an amshu-vimarda (a collision of rays -- the discs themselves do not touch): center-to-center separation 0°41′01.51″, 0°40′56.65″ apart, disc-to-disc. aṅgārakaḥ at uttarāṣāḍhā-4 makaraḥ (latitude 1°06′36.21″ S, Rju (direct), magnitude +1.17, elongation 16°01′11.81″ E). budhaḥ at uttarāṣāḍhā-4 makaraḥ (latitude 1°47′37.72″ S, Rju (direct), magnitude -0.85, elongation 16°04′48.67″ E). Classical texts weigh both the northern position and the greater apparent brightness/nearness in deciding the victor (jayI) of a yuddha; here budhaḥ is towards the north (traditionally said to prevail), while by brightness/nearness (the larger apparent diameter) budhaḥ is taken as jayI over aṅgārakaḥ. A graha-yuddha (also called amshu-vimarda, "collision of rays") occurs when two of the five tArA grahas -- budha, śukra, aṅgāraka, br̥haspati, śanaiśchara -- come within 1 aMsha (60 kalA) of each other in longitude, close enough that they may be difficult to tell apart in the sky. It is called yuddha proper only when their discs actually touch/overlap; otherwise, amshu-vimarda.

The Surya Siddhanta itself cautions that this matter is described only to indicate the auspicious/inauspicious effects for people -- in reality the grahas remain far apart from one another and continue along their own paths. This is not to be received with fear, but as an advance, compassionate intimation from those who calculated these movements accurately, meant to help people take protective measures in time.

Classical texts (e.g. Brihat Samhita ch. 17) weigh both which graha is to the north and which is more prominent (nearer/brighter, of larger apparent diameter) in declaring a victor (jayī) of the yuddha; the defeated (jita) graha's significations are said to suffer for a particular section of society -- this is never a universal ill effect. The traditional response is to increase one's spiritual efforts: japa, homa, dAna and parAyaNa (especially of the Navagraha stotra), with higher AvRtti for the two grahas actually involved, particularly if the day also coincides with some other puNya kAla (e.g. a sAyana saGkramaNa).

Per the Narada Samhita (as cited in Muhurta Chintamani), the nakshatra in which a graha-yuddha occurs should be avoided for auspicious functions (vivAha, upanayana etc.) for six months following the event. If this cannot be avoided, perform parihAra for candra-bala.

8ba5c0df09.b: Event occured on 1681-02-10 (gregorian). Julian date was converted to Gregorian in this reckoning.
8ba5c0df09.d:
Barely 15 days after being crowned in a grand ceremony at Raigad fort, Maratha army commanded by Sambhaji and Hambirrao Mohite attacked and plundered the city for three days. The Marathas got a huge loot (around 2 crore Rs) and returned to Raigad by evading Mughal forces.

Sambhaji had got the news that Bahadurkhan Kokaltash, the Subedar of Burhanpur was going to Aurangabad for his nephew's wedding with a girl Qutb Shah family. Bahadurkhan took a force 3,000 with him for the wedding. Hence Burhanpur was left with an army of 5,000 under Kakar Khan (in charge of collecting jizya tax). Sambhaji and his generals decided to further bifurcate the force at Burhanpur by feigning a move to attack Surat, forcing the Mughals at Burhanpur to send reinforcement to Surat, which had been sacked by Shivaji twice before.

Hambirrao Mohite reached the forests near Burhanpur with a 15,000 strong cavalry force. Kakar Khan gathered civilian forces and decided to attack Hambirrao at midnight. As he came out of the city gates, Sambhaji himself attacked from the old trenches with a cavalry force of 4,000. Sambhaji's force routed the ill-prepared Mughal garrison. Sambhaji then left 200-300 soldiers at the main city gate and left for Bahadurpura, the richest suburb of the city. Sambhaji started to loot the houses of the richest merchants which were shown to him by his spies. Hambirrao's force soon joined Sambhaji and the combined Maratha force started looting the city. Hambirrao then sealed the city's entrances to ensure that the word of the attack doesn't spread out. Marathas looted the city consecutively for three days.

Bahadurkhan hurried from Aurangabad with a large army and tried to recover the loot, but he was foiled by sambhAjI's tactics. Meanwhile, Suryaji Jakhde took advantage of this to briefly attack Aurangabad with a force of 7,000 via Paithan; and bahAdurkhAn had to return anyway. Some of Awrangzeb's elite Ahadi horsemen (stationed in every mogol city) tried to assassinate sambhAjI when he was visiting Saptashringi temple at vani on his way back - but failed.

8be82e6dae.b: Graha-yuddha (amshu-vimarda) between guruḥ and budhaḥ in puṣyaḥ karkaṭaḥ, center-to-center separation 0°33′10.25″.
8be82e6dae.d:
This is an amshu-vimarda (a collision of rays -- the discs themselves do not touch): center-to-center separation 0°33′10.25″, 0°32′52.10″ apart, disc-to-disc. guruḥ at puṣyaḥ-4 karkaṭaḥ (latitude 0°29′56.87″ N, Rju (direct), magnitude -1.79, elongation 12°31′32.41″ W). budhaḥ at puṣyaḥ-4 karkaṭaḥ (latitude 1°03′07.12″ N, Rju (direct), magnitude -1.26, elongation 12°33′33.68″ W). Classical texts weigh both the northern position and the greater apparent brightness/nearness in deciding the victor (jayI) of a yuddha; here budhaḥ is towards the north (traditionally said to prevail), while by brightness/nearness (the larger apparent diameter) guruḥ is taken as jayI over budhaḥ. A graha-yuddha (also called amshu-vimarda, "collision of rays") occurs when two of the five tArA grahas -- budha, śukra, aṅgāraka, br̥haspati, śanaiśchara -- come within 1 aMsha (60 kalA) of each other in longitude, close enough that they may be difficult to tell apart in the sky. It is called yuddha proper only when their discs actually touch/overlap; otherwise, amshu-vimarda.

The Surya Siddhanta itself cautions that this matter is described only to indicate the auspicious/inauspicious effects for people -- in reality the grahas remain far apart from one another and continue along their own paths. This is not to be received with fear, but as an advance, compassionate intimation from those who calculated these movements accurately, meant to help people take protective measures in time.

Classical texts (e.g. Brihat Samhita ch. 17) weigh both which graha is to the north and which is more prominent (nearer/brighter, of larger apparent diameter) in declaring a victor (jayī) of the yuddha; the defeated (jita) graha's significations are said to suffer for a particular section of society -- this is never a universal ill effect. The traditional response is to increase one's spiritual efforts: japa, homa, dAna and parAyaNa (especially of the Navagraha stotra), with higher AvRtti for the two grahas actually involved, particularly if the day also coincides with some other puNya kAla (e.g. a sAyana saGkramaNa).

Per the Narada Samhita (as cited in Muhurta Chintamani), the nakshatra in which a graha-yuddha occurs should be avoided for auspicious functions (vivAha, upanayana etc.) for six months following the event. If this cannot be avoided, perform parihAra for candra-bala.
